```{r setup}
# The 30-45 minute talk: the data-sources deck and the analysis (Ghana) deck combined,
# with the illustrated concept slides drawn in place by scripts/concept_slides/ from
# MN-proxy-full-talk-2026-09.concept.yaml. Every figure is drawn from the result tables
# at render time, every number in the text, the notes AND the concept slides is an
# expression over the same `Q` list below, so a pipeline re-run followed by
#   bash scripts/render_deck.sh docs/slides/MN-proxy-full-talk-2026-09.qmd --text 18,10 \
#        --concept docs/slides/MN-proxy-full-talk-2026-09.concept.yaml
# refreshes the whole deck. Concept slides are a title plus speaker notes here; their
# content lives in the YAML. The setup is the Ghana deck's chunk followed by the
# data-sources deck's additions (tiers, alignment, spine, exclusions, recurrence).
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(knitr); library(ggplot2)})
root <- tryCatch(here::here(), error = function(e) normalizePath(file.path(getwd(), "..", "..")))
P2 <- file.path(root, "results", "tables", "protocol_v2")
CL <- file.path(root, "results", "tables", "cluster_level")
rd <- function(...) { f <- file.path(...); if (file.exists(f)) read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE) else NULL }
kb <- function(d, digits = 3, ...) knitr::kable(d, format = "pipe", digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, ...)
df <- function(...) data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
f2 <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.finite(x), formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "NA")
pc <- function(x, d = 0) ifelse(is.finite(x), paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%"), "NA")
sgn <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.finite(x), paste0(ifelse(x >= 0, "+", ""), formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)), "NA")
get1 <- function(x) if (length(x) && is.finite(x[1])) unname(x[1]) else NA_real_   # unname: a quantile() name would make the JSON value an object

# mean over cells with a 95% interval across cells (normal approximation over the cell values)
cell_ci <- function(d, val, by) {
  d |> group_by(across(all_of(by))) |>
    summarise(n = sum(is.finite(.data[[val]])), est = mean(.data[[val]], na.rm = TRUE),
              se = sd(.data[[val]], na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(pmax(n, 1)), lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se,
              pos = sum(.data[[val]] > 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}
forest <- function(d, y, facet = NULL, null = 0, xlab = "Spearman (mean over cells, 95% interval)", base = 15, colour = NULL) {
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = est, y = .data[[y]])) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = null, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, colour = "grey35", orientation = "y")
  g <- if (is.null(colour)) g + geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f4e79") else g + geom_point(aes(colour = .data[[colour]]), size = 3)
  g <- g + labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = base) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
  if (!is.null(facet)) g <- g + facet_wrap(as.formula(paste("~", facet)), scales = "free_x")
  g
}
tlab <- c(level = "Biomarker level", prev = "Prevalence")
olab <- c(child_vitA = "Child vitamin A", women_vitA = "Women's vitamin A", child_iron = "Child iron", women_iron = "Women's iron",
          women_folate = "Women's folate", women_b12 = "Women's B12", child_zinc = "Child zinc", women_zinc = "Women's zinc")
arm_label <- c(domain_index = "Zero-tuning domain index", spatial_plus_domain = "Spatial smoother + covariates", spatial = "Spatial smoother",
               domain_enet = "Elastic net, domain components", raw_enet = "Elastic net, all columns",
               region_mean_jk = "Jackknifed regional mean", null_train_mean = "Training mean")

MD  <- rd(root, "data", "covariates", "harmonized", "predictors_admin2_shared_metadata.csv")
BM  <- rd(P2, "benchmarks_v2_summary.csv"); BC <- rd(P2, "benchmarks_v2_cells.csv")
A1  <- rd(P2, "admin1_transport.csv"); CS1 <- rd(P2, "climate_soil_admin1.csv"); ND <- rd(P2, "nested_domain_selection.csv"); NC <- rd(P2, "transport_null_calibration.csv")
WS  <- rd(P2, "weight_sources_cells.csv"); NT <- rd(P2, "nce_targeting_metrics.csv"); NTS <- rd(P2, "nce_targeting_summary.csv")
DA  <- rd(P2, "domain_ablation_loco.csv"); SA <- rd(P2, "source_ablation_loco.csv"); SAS <- rd(P2, "source_ablation_loco_summary.csv")
TC  <- rd(P2, "training_country_curve.csv"); TCS <- rd(P2, "training_curve_climate_soil.csv")
UR  <- rd(P2, "urbanicity_conditioning.csv"); VC <- rd(P2, "variance_components_ceiling.csv"); AR <- rd(P2, "anchor_and_rank.csv")
CV  <- rd(CL, "cluster_vs_district.csv"); MBG <- rd(CL, "mbg_comparison_cells.csv"); TCLU <- rd(CL, "targets_cluster.csv")
RC  <- rd(P2, "risk_category_accuracy.csv"); IL <- rd(P2, "individual_level_models.csv"); IO <- rd(P2, "iodine_in_country.csv")
IT  <- rd(P2, "index_importance_top.csv"); IP <- rd(P2, "index_importance_patterns.csv"); ID <- rd(P2, "index_importance_domains.csv")
TG  <- rd(P2, "targets_v2.csv"); SY <- rd(root, "metadata", "survey_years.csv"); NE <- rd(root, "results", "tables", "national_estimates_all.csv")
SLR <- rd(P2, "sl_rank_loss_scores.csv"); SLH <- rd(P2, "sl_domain_index_scores_hapc.csv"); LI <- rd(P2, "addon_lsms_flunet_infill.csv")
SIG <- rd(root, "results", "tables", "signal_probes", "p4_admin1_continuous_predictors.csv")

# ---- quantities used in the text -------------------------------------------------------
Q <- list()
bm <- function(est, tg, arm, col = "mean_spearman") if (is.null(BM)) NA_real_ else get1(BM[[col]][BM$estimand == est & BM$target == tg & BM$arm == arm])
Q$n_pred <- if (is.null(MD)) NA else nrow(MD); Q$n_dom <- if (is.null(MD)) NA else length(unique(MD$domain))
Q$n_cells <- if (is.null(TG)) NA else nrow(distinct(TG, country, outcome))
Q$n_districts <- if (is.null(TG)) NA else nrow(distinct(TG, country, Admin1, Admin2))
Q$n_clusters <- if (is.null(TCLU)) NA else nrow(distinct(TCLU, country, cluster))
Q$infill_index <- bm("infill", "level", "domain_index"); Q$infill_index_p <- bm("infill", "prev", "domain_index")
Q$infill_jk <- bm("infill", "level", "region_mean_jk"); Q$infill_jk_p <- bm("infill", "prev", "region_mean_jk")
Q$infill_sp <- bm("infill", "level", "spatial"); Q$infill_spd <- bm("infill", "level", "spatial_plus_domain")
Q$infill_enet <- bm("infill", "level", "domain_enet"); Q$infill_raw <- bm("infill", "level", "raw_enet")
Q$region_index <- bm("region", "level", "domain_index"); Q$region_index_p <- bm("region", "prev", "domain_index")
Q$region_sp <- bm("region", "level", "spatial"); Q$region_enet_p <- bm("region", "prev", "domain_enet"); Q$region_raw_p <- bm("region", "prev", "raw_enet")
Q$tr_index <- bm("country", "level", "domain_index"); Q$tr_index_p <- bm("country", "prev", "domain_index")
Q$tr_index_pos <- bm("country", "level", "domain_index", "cells_positive"); Q$tr_index_pos_p <- bm("country", "prev", "domain_index", "cells_positive")
Q$tr_enet <- bm("country", "level", "domain_enet"); Q$tr_enet_pos <- bm("country", "level", "domain_enet", "cells_positive")
Q$tr_cells <- bm("country", "level", "domain_index", "cells")
Q$tr_a1 <- if (is.null(A1)) NA else get1(mean(A1$spearman[A1$arm == "domain_index" & A1$target == "level"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$tr_a1_p <- if (is.null(A1)) NA else get1(mean(A1$spearman[A1$arm == "domain_index" & A1$target == "prev"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$tr_a1_pos <- if (is.null(A1)) NA else sum(A1$spearman[A1$arm == "domain_index" & A1$target == "level"] > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
Q$cs_d <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else get1(mean(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "fixed_cs" & ND$target == "level"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$cs_d_pos <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else sum(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "fixed_cs" & ND$target == "level"] > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
Q$cs_d_p <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else get1(mean(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "fixed_cs" & ND$target == "prev"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$cs_a1 <- if (is.null(CS1)) NA else get1(mean(CS1$spearman[CS1$set == "climate_soil" & CS1$target == "level"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$cs_a1_pos <- if (is.null(CS1)) NA else sum(CS1$spearman[CS1$set == "climate_soil" & CS1$target == "level"] > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
Q$nested_vs_full <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else { w <- ND |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% c("full", "nested")) |> select(outcome, heldout, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman); get1(median(w$nested - w$full, na.rm = TRUE)) }
Q$cs5_d <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else get1(mean(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "fixed_cs_top5" & ND$target == "level"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$cs5_d_p <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else get1(mean(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "fixed_cs_top5" & ND$target == "prev"], na.rm = TRUE))
Q$nested_d <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else get1(mean(ND$spearman[ND$arm == "nested" & ND$target == "level"], na.rm = TRUE))
if (!is.null(ND) && "fixed_cs_top5" %in% ND$arm) { w5 <- ND |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% c("fixed_cs", "fixed_cs_top5")) |> select(outcome, heldout, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman)
  Q$cs5_better <- sum(w5$fixed_cs_top5 > w5$fixed_cs, na.rm = TRUE); Q$cs5_delta <- get1(median(w5$fixed_cs_top5 - w5$fixed_cs, na.rm = TRUE)) }
Q$nested_better <- if (is.null(ND)) NA else { w <- ND |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% c("full", "nested")) |> select(outcome, heldout, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman); sum(w$nested > w$full, na.rm = TRUE) }
Q$null_d <- if (is.null(NC)) NA else get1(NC$null_mean_q95[NC$tier == "admin2"]); Q$null_a1 <- if (is.null(NC)) NA else get1(NC$null_mean_q95[NC$tier == "admin1"])
Q$null_pos95 <- if (is.null(NC)) NA else get1(NC$null_positive_q95[NC$tier == "admin2"])
# in-fill: index vs jackknifed regional mean, cells better (level)
if (!is.null(BC)) { w <- BC |> filter(estimand == "infill", target == "level", arm %in% c("domain_index", "region_mean_jk", "spatial")) |> select(country, outcome, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman)
  Q$infill_beats_jk <- sum(w$domain_index > w$region_mean_jk, na.rm = TRUE); Q$infill_paired <- sum(is.finite(w$domain_index - w$region_mean_jk)); Q$infill_index_minus_sp <- get1(mean(w$domain_index - w$spatial, na.rm = TRUE)) }
# geostatistical comparator
if (!is.null(MBG)) { m <- MBG |> filter(estimand == "infill") |> group_by(target, arm) |> summarise(v = mean(rho_agg, na.rm = TRUE), w = mean(wmae_agg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  gm <- function(tg, a, col = "v") get1(m[[col]][m$target == tg & m$arm == a])
  Q$mbg_index <- gm("level", "domain_index"); Q$mbg_mbg <- gm("level", "mbg"); Q$mbg_dhs <- gm("level", "mbg_dhs"); Q$mbg_gp <- gm("level", "mbg_gp")
  Q$mbg_index_p <- gm("prev", "domain_index"); Q$mbg_mbg_p <- gm("prev", "mbg"); Q$mbg_w_index <- gm("prev", "domain_index", "w"); Q$mbg_w_mbg <- gm("prev", "mbg", "w")
  w2 <- MBG |> filter(estimand == "infill", target == "level", arm %in% c("domain_index", "mbg")) |> select(country, outcome, arm, rho_agg) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = rho_agg)
  Q$mbg_index_better <- sum(w2$domain_index > w2$mbg, na.rm = TRUE); Q$mbg_cells <- sum(is.finite(w2$domain_index - w2$mbg))
  mr <- MBG |> filter(estimand == "region", target == "level") |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(v = mean(rho_agg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  Q$mbg_region_index <- get1(mr$v[mr$arm == "domain_index"]); Q$mbg_region_mbg <- get1(mr$v[mr$arm == "mbg"]) }
# weight sources: paired against the index
if (!is.null(WS)) { w <- WS |> filter(estimand == "country", target == "level") |> select(country, outcome, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman)
  pd <- function(a) c(d = get1(mean(w[[a]] - w$domain_index, na.rm = TRUE)), b = sum(w[[a]] > w$domain_index, na.rm = TRUE), n = sum(is.finite(w[[a]] - w$domain_index)))
  Q$ws_decor <- pd("index_decor"); Q$ws_sparse20 <- pd("sparse20"); Q$ws_soft1 <- pd("index_soft1"); Q$ws_enet <- pd("domain_enet"); Q$ws_ridge <- pd("ridge_min")
  wi <- WS |> filter(estimand == "infill", target == "level") |> select(country, outcome, arm, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = spearman)
  pdi <- function(a) get1(mean(wi[[a]] - wi$domain_index, na.rm = TRUE))
  Q$wsi_ridge <- pdi("ridge_min"); Q$wsi_enet <- pdi("domain_enet"); Q$wsi_lasso <- pdi("lasso_min"); Q$wsi_decor <- pdi("index_decor"); Q$wsi_sparse20 <- pdi("sparse20"); Q$wsi_sparse5 <- pdi("sparse5")
  Q$ws_1se_scored <- if (!is.null(WS)) sum(is.finite(WS$spearman[WS$estimand == "country" & WS$target == "level" & WS$arm == "enet_1se"])) else NA }
# targeting
if (!is.null(NTS)) { nt <- NTS |> filter(estimand == "infill"); Q$cap_index <- get1(nt$mean_capture[nt$arm == "domain_index"]); Q$cap_jk <- get1(nt$mean_capture[nt$arm == "region_mean_jk"]); Q$cap_null <- get1(nt$mean_capture[nt$arm == "null_train_mean"]); Q$cap_oracle <- get1(nt$mean_capture[nt$arm == "oracle_ceiling"]) }
# ablation
abl_delta <- function(X, unit) {   # per cell: full-model Spearman (row "ALL") minus the value with the unit dropped
  full <- X |> filter(variant == "full", .data[[unit]] == "ALL") |> select(target, outcome, heldout, full = spearman)
  X |> filter(variant == "drop", .data[[unit]] != "ALL") |> inner_join(full, by = c("target", "outcome", "heldout")) |> mutate(delta = full - spearman)
}
if (!is.null(DA)) { das <- abl_delta(DA, "domain") |> filter(target == "level") |> group_by(domain) |> summarise(delta = mean(delta, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(desc(delta))
  Q$da_top <- head(das, 5); Q$da_neg <- sum(das$delta <= 0); Q$da_n <- nrow(das) }
if (!is.null(SA)) { sas <- abl_delta(SA, "source") |> filter(target == "level") |> group_by(source) |> summarise(full = mean(full, na.rm = TRUE), drop = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  Q$sa_dhs_full <- get1(sas$full[sas$source == "DHS"]); Q$sa_dhs_drop <- get1(sas$drop[sas$source == "DHS"]); Q$sa_dhs_cols <- if (is.null(SAS)) NA else get1(SAS$n_cols[SAS$source == "DHS" & SAS$target == "level"])
  im <- grepl("^MICS microdata", sas$source); Q$sa_mics <- get1(sas$full[im] - sas$drop[im]); Q$sa_mics_cols <- if (is.null(SAS)) NA else get1(SAS$n_cols[grepl("^MICS microdata", SAS$source) & SAS$target == "level"]) }
# RR-11 (2026-09-16): the headline set has no DHS; the with-DHS and open-only transport arms are read from their own summaries
BMD <- rd(P2, "benchmarks_v2_summary_withdhs.csv"); BMO <- rd(P2, "benchmarks_v2_summary_open.csv")
bmx <- function(X, est, tg, arm) if (is.null(X)) NA_real_ else get1(X$mean_spearman[X$estimand == est & X$target == tg & X$arm == arm])
Q$tr_dhs <- bmx(BMD, "country", "level", "domain_index"); Q$tr_dhs_p <- bmx(BMD, "country", "prev", "domain_index")
Q$tr_open <- bmx(BMO, "country", "level", "domain_index"); Q$tr_open_p <- bmx(BMO, "country", "prev", "domain_index")
Q$n_dhs <- if (is.null(MD)) NA else sum(MD$source == "DHS"); Q$n_head <- if (is.null(MD) || !"tier" %in% names(MD)) NA else sum(MD$tier %in% c("open", "survey_public") & as.logical(toupper(as.character(MD$subnational))))
# training curve slope
if (!is.null(TC)) { tcm <- TC |> filter(arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> group_by(n_train_countries) |> summarise(v = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); Q$tc_slope <- get1((tcm$v[tcm$n_train_countries == 3] - tcm$v[tcm$n_train_countries == 1]) / 2) }
if (!is.null(TCS)) { tcc <- TCS |> filter(set == "climate_soil", target == "level"); Q$tcs_pos1 <- get1(mean(tcc$spearman[tcc$n_train_countries == 1] > 0, na.rm = TRUE)) }
# urbanicity
if (!is.null(UR)) { u <- UR |> filter(target == "level", tier == "admin2"); Q$ur_cs <- mean(u$rho_cs, na.rm = TRUE); Q$ur_partial <- mean(u$partial_cs, na.rm = TRUE); Q$ur_only <- mean(u$rho_urb_only, na.rm = TRUE) }
# ceiling
if (!is.null(VC)) { v <- VC |> filter(rung == "admin2", target == "prev"); Q$vc_honest <- mean(v$ceiling_vc, na.rm = TRUE); Q$vc_split <- mean(v$ceiling_within_vc, na.rm = TRUE); Q$vc_share <- mean(v$cluster_share_of_ceiling, na.rm = TRUE); Q$vc_at <- sum(v$achieved_spearman >= v$ceiling_vc, na.rm = TRUE); Q$vc_n <- sum(is.finite(v$ceiling_vc)) }
# survey design
if (!is.null(AR)) { a <- AR |> filter(rank_from == "prev", set == "climate_soil", fraction == 0.05) |> group_by(design) |> summarise(mae = median(mae, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  Q$ar_a1 <- get1(a$mae[a$design == "A1_anchor_rank"]); Q$ar_c <- get1(a$mae[a$design == "C_regional_survey"]); Q$ar_b <- get1(a$mae[a$design == "B_district_survey"])
  b <- AR |> filter(rank_from == "prev", set == "climate_soil", design == "B_district_survey") |> group_by(fraction) |> summarise(mae = median(mae, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); Q$ar_b_match <- get1(min(b$fraction[b$mae <= Q$ar_a1])) }
# cluster track
if (!is.null(CV)) { cvm <- CV |> filter(set == "transportable", arm == "domain_index", estimand == "infill", target == "level"); Q$cv_agg <- mean(cvm$rho_agg, na.rm = TRUE); Q$cv_dist <- mean(cvm$rho_district_v2, na.rm = TRUE) }
# risk classes
if (!is.null(RC)) { r <- RC |> filter(scheme == "who_vitA") |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(ex = mean(exact_admin2, na.rm = TRUE), w1 = mean(within1_admin2, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); Q$rc_ex <- get1(r$ex[r$arm == "domain_index"]); Q$rc_w1 <- get1(r$w1[r$arm == "domain_index"]) }
# individual level
if (!is.null(IL)) { i <- IL |> group_by(set) |> summarise(auc = mean(auc, na.rm = TRUE), bs = mean(brier_skill, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); Q$il_auc_s <- get1(i$auc[i$set == "survey_only"]); Q$il_auc_p <- get1(i$auc[i$set == "proxies_only"]); Q$il_auc_b <- get1(i$auc[i$set == "both"]); Q$il_bs_max <- max(i$bs, na.rm = TRUE); Q$il_cells <- sum(IL$set == "survey_only")
  ir <- IL |> filter(grepl("iron", outcome), set == "survey_only"); Q$il_iron_max <- max(ir$auc, na.rm = TRUE); Q$il_iron_min_top <- get1(sort(ir$auc, decreasing = TRUE)[3]) }
# SuperLearner comparisons (rank loss run: index, rank ensembles, random forest, mse ensembles)
if (!is.null(SLR)) { s <- SLR |> filter(arm %in% c("domain_index", "rank_nnls", "rf", "mse_nnls", "enet")) |> group_by(country, outcome, arm) |> summarise(sp = median(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = sp); s <- s[stats::complete.cases(s), ]   # the cells every arm scored
  sl <- function(a) get1(mean(s[[a]], na.rm = TRUE)); Q$sl_index <- sl("domain_index"); Q$sl_rank <- sl("rank_nnls"); Q$sl_rf <- sl("rf"); Q$sl_mse <- sl("mse_nnls"); Q$sl_enet <- sl("enet"); Q$sl_cells <- nrow(s) }
if (!is.null(SLH)) { s <- SLH |> group_by(country, outcome, arm) |> summarise(sp = median(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(v = mean(sp, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); Q$sl_hapc <- get1(s$v[s$arm == "hapc"]) }
# importance shares
if (!is.null(ID)) { e <- ID |> filter(scope == "pooled", target == "level") |> group_by(outcome) |> summarise(env = sum(share[domain %in% c("Satellite embedding", "Climate and weather", "Soil characteristics")]), .groups = "drop"); Q$env_lo <- min(e$env); Q$env_hi <- max(e$env) }
if (!is.null(IT)) { ci20 <- IT |> filter(outcome == "child_iron", target == "level", rank <= 20); Q$ci_rep <- sum(ci20$incountry_sign_agree == ci20$incountry_fits); Q$ci_loco <- sum(ci20$loco_sign_agree == ci20$loco_fits) }

`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a
FIG <- "../../results/figures/policy_deck"; GREY <- "grey65"; BLUE <- "#1f4e79"; LIGHT <- "#6baed6"
source(file.path(root, "R", "predictor_plain_names.R"))   # PLAIN, clean_code()
tier_lab <- c(open = "Open data", survey_public = "Public survey microdata", survey_dhs = "DHS (access agreement)")
tier_col <- c(`Open data` = BLUE, `Public survey microdata` = LIGHT, `DHS (access agreement)` = GREY)

# metadata file on disk, matched against metadata/covariates/exclusions.csv (built = in the set + excluded)
built_excluded <- function() {
  if (is.null(MD) || is.null(EX)) return(NULL)
  HD <- file.path(root, "data", "covariates", "harmonized")
  fs <- c(list.files(HD, pattern = "^predictors_admin2_shared_metadata[.]csv[.]pre_", full.names = TRUE), list.files(HD, pattern = "^predictors_admin2_[a-z_]+_metadata[.]csv$", full.names = TRUE))
  u <- MD[, c("column", "source")]
  for (f in fs) { m <- tryCatch(read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL); if (!is.null(m) && all(c("column", "source") %in% names(m))) u <- rbind(u, m[!m$column %in% u$column, c("column", "source")]) }
  u <- u[!duplicated(u$column), ]; gone <- u[!u$column %in% MD$column, ]
  hit <- vapply(gone$column, function(cc) any(vapply(EX$canonical_regex, function(rx) grepl(rx, cc, perl = TRUE), NA)), NA)
  gone[hit, ]
}

clab <- c(Gambia = "The Gambia", Ghana = "Ghana", Malawi = "Malawi", SierraLeone = "Sierra Leone")
cell_label <- function(country, outcome) { o <- olab[outcome]; paste0(clab[country], ": ", tolower(substr(o, 1, 1)), substr(o, 2, nchar(o))) }
CELL <- if (is.null(BR)) NULL else BR |> filter(is.finite(spearman) | is.finite(wmae)) |> group_by(country, outcome, target, estimand, arm) |>
  summarise(reps = n(), across(c(spearman, wmae, rmse_sd, pearson), list(m = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), se = ~ ifelse(n() > 1, sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()), NA_real_))), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(cell = cell_label(country, outcome))
STRONG_CUT <- 0.5
if (!is.null(CELL)) {   # the strong cells: index in-fill Spearman on the level at or above the cut
  ix <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> arrange(desc(spearman_m))
  ixp <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "prev") |> select(country, outcome, sp_prev = spearman_m, wmae_prev = wmae_m)
  ix <- ix |> left_join(ixp, by = c("country", "outcome"))
  if (!is.null(NT)) { pn <- NT |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index") |> group_by(country, outcome) |> summarise(prev_nat = mean(prev_national, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"); ix <- ix |> left_join(pn, by = c("country", "outcome")) }
  Q$strong_n <- sum(ix$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT, na.rm = TRUE); Q$strong_of <- sum(is.finite(ix$spearman_m)); Q$strong_cut <- STRONG_CUT
  Q$strong_mean <- get1(mean(ix$spearman_m[ix$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], na.rm = TRUE)); Q$weak_mean <- get1(mean(ix$spearman_m[ix$spearman_m < STRONG_CUT], na.rm = TRUE))
  Q$strong_pairs <- (1 + 2 / pi * asin(Q$strong_mean)) / 2   # approximation; the exact per-cell count is in nce_targeting_metrics.csv
  for (k in 1:4) { r <- ix[k, ]; Q[[paste0("best", k, "_label")]] <- r$cell; Q[[paste0("best", k, "_rho")]] <- r$spearman_m; Q[[paste0("best", k, "_rho_prev")]] <- r$sp_prev
    Q[[paste0("best", k, "_wmae")]] <- r$wmae_prev; Q[[paste0("best", k, "_prev")]] <- r$prev_nat; Q[[paste0("best", k, "_n")]] <- r$reps }
  rare <- ix |> filter(is.finite(prev_nat), prev_nat < 0.01); Q$rare_n <- nrow(rare); Q$rare_mean <- get1(mean(rare$spearman_m, na.rm = TRUE))
  Q$zinc_mean <- get1(mean(ix$spearman_m[grepl("zinc", ix$outcome)], na.rm = TRUE))
  gm <- ix$spearman_m[ix$country == "Gambia"]; Q$gambia_min <- get1(min(gm)); Q$gambia_max <- get1(max(gm)); Q$gambia_cells <- sum(is.finite(gm)); Q$gambia_strong <- sum(gm >= STRONG_CUT, na.rm = TRUE)
  om <- ix$spearman_m[ix$country != "Gambia"]; Q$other_mean <- get1(mean(om, na.rm = TRUE)); Q$other_strong <- sum(om >= STRONG_CUT, na.rm = TRUE); Q$other_cells <- sum(is.finite(om))
  Q$gambia_clusters_per_district <- if (is.finite(Q$clusters_Gambia %||% NA) && is.finite(Q$districts_Gambia %||% NA)) Q$clusters_Gambia / Q$districts_Gambia else NA
```

## Goals

::: {.notes}
The three project goals as stated in the proposal: district and national prevalence estimates from proxies, validated against biomarker surveys; the districts at greatest risk; engagement with national stakeholders throughout. The map is Ghana child iron deficiency from the 2017 survey, the worked example that recurs through the talk.
:::

## What does a country have today, and what does the model add?

```{r before-after, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.9, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  B <- sf::st_as_sf(readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["ghana"]])
  t <- TG[TG$country == "Ghana" & TG$outcome == "child_vitA" & is.finite(TG$y_prev), c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "n_raw")]
  nat <- weighted.mean(t$y_prev, t$n_raw); reg <- t |> group_by(Admin1) |> summarise(v = weighted.mean(y_prev, n_raw), .groups = "drop")
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, reg, by = "Admin1"); g$national <- nat
  m <- if (!is.null(EXC)) dplyr::left_join(B, EXC[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "pred_med")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2")) else NULL
  sc <- scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#fff7ec", "#fdd49e", "#fc8d59", "#d7301f", "#7f0000"), limits = c(0, 0.6), oob = scales::oob_squish, labels = scales::percent, na.value = "grey90", name = NULL)
  th <- theme_void(base_size = 13) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30"), legend.position = "none")
  p1 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = national), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "Between surveys: one national number", subtitle = sprintf("child vitamin A deficiency %.0f%% everywhere", 100 * nat)) + th
  p2 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = v), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "From the survey: regional (Admin-1) estimates", subtitle = sprintf("%d regions, one value each", nrow(reg))) + th
  p3 <- ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred_med), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "From the model: every district", subtitle = sprintf("%d districts, %d never surveyed", nrow(m), sum(!EXC$surveyed))) + th + theme(legend.position = "right")
  arrow <- ggplot() + annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 1, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed"), colour = "#1f4e79", linewidth = 1.4) + xlim(-0.2, 1.2) + theme_void()
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, arrow, p2, arrow, p3, ncol = 5, widths = c(1, 0.18, 1, 0.18, 1.25))); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: This is the whole talk in one picture, using child vitamin A deficiency in Ghana. Between surveys a program has one national number. The survey itself gives an estimate per region, which is what it was designed to do. The model gives a value for every district, including the 185 the survey never reached. The rest of the talk is about how far that right-hand map can be trusted.

DETAIL: Left: the national prevalence from the 2017 survey applied everywhere. Middle: respondent-weighted averages over the 16 regions on the 2019 boundaries (the survey was designed for the 10 old regions). Right: the index fitted on the 75 surveyed districts and applied to all 260 (median over 200 resampled refits, the exceedance slide's table). The national surveys do give Admin-1 estimates; what they cannot give is every Admin-2, which is the model's job. Warm palette on a shared 0-60% scale.
:::

## Surveys are rare; the proxies are everywhere

::: {.notes}
Photo credit: Latter-day Saint Charities. GMS 2017 collaborators: University of Ghana, GroundWork, University of Wisconsin-Madison, KEMRI-Wellcome Trust; with UNICEF and Global Affairs Canada.
:::

## Both a big-data opportunity and a small-data problem

::: {.notes}
SAY: The same project is both. The opportunity: hundreds of public layers covering every district. The problem: the thing we predict is measured once a decade, in 14 to 87 districts per country. Everything in the protocol follows from holding both at once.

DETAIL: The same sentence describes both halves. Big: `r Q$n_pred` columns from `r Q$n_src` sources, most of them rasters at 30 m to 10 km summarized over `r nrow(SP)` districts, four household surveys aggregated from their microdata, a satellite embedding with 64 dimensions per district. Small: the thing being predicted is measured in one biomarker survey per country per decade, at `r Q$n_districts` surveyed districts over four countries, `r Q$n_cells` country-outcome outcome-country combinations, and 14 to 87 districts per country, which is the effective sample size of every model. Everything in the protocol follows from holding both at once: predictors are reduced to domain components with nothing chosen on the outcome, the estimator has no tuned parameter, the folds are cut by district, region and country, and the reliability ceiling says how much of the survey signal is noise at district level. Likely question: why not fit at the person level. That was the January approach; a person-level classifier under district-blocked folds is a coin toss on proxies alone, and shrinking its predictions biases area means (individual-level slide in the appendix).
:::

```{r survey-maps, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.6, dpi=140}
  for (cn in names(LC)) {
    B <- sf::st_as_sf(BND[[LC[[cn]]]]) |> group_by(Admin1) |> summarise(geometry = sf::st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop")
    t <- TG[TG$country == cn & TG$outcome == "women_iron" & is.finite(TG$y_prev), ] |> group_by(Admin1) |> summarise(v = weighted.mean(y_prev, n_raw), .groups = "drop")
    g <- dplyr::left_join(B, t, by = "Admin1")
    lab <- sprintf("%s %s\n%d districts, %d clusters", clab[cn], Q[[paste0("year_", cn)]], Q[[paste0("districts_", cn)]], Q[[paste0("clusters_", cn)]])
    maps[[cn]] <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = v), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.8), na.value = "grey90", name = "Women's iron\ndeficiency") +
      labs(title = lab) + theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5)) }
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(maps, ncol = 4) + patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "right")); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Four national micronutrient surveys, one per country, each with blood biomarkers and GPS clusters: The Gambia 2018, Ghana 2017, Sierra Leone 2013, Malawi 2015-16. The maps show women's iron deficiency by region as the surveys report it; the districts and clusters under each map are what the model learns from.

DETAIL: Region-level respondent-weighted prevalence of women's iron deficiency from targets_v2.csv, on the GADM 4.1 regions. Counts per country from the same table and the cluster file (Sierra Leone: 14 districts, 60 clusters; The Gambia 30 and 70; Ghana 75 and 90; Malawi 87 and 103). All four measured iron and vitamin A in children and women; folate and B12 in three (not The Gambia); zinc in Malawi only. Fieldwork dates recovered for every cluster; three surveys ran in the dry season and Malawi in the lean season. Likely question: why districts rather than regions. Districts are the program unit; they sit below the surveys' design resolution, which is why the reliability ceiling slide reports what a perfect predictor could reach.
:::

## Which deficiencies do we predict?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Five deficiencies, each defined once, the same way in every country, reconciled against the survey reports: iron, vitamin A, folate, B12 and zinc. Children under five and non-pregnant women.

DETAIL: Two targets per outcome-country combination: the deficiency prevalence, and the district mean of the negated log biomarker concentration (higher means worse), which carries more signal than the dichotomy and is reported alongside it. Definitions were reconciled against the four survey reports and the 21 papers that re-analyze them on 15 September 2026 (docs/survey_report_reconciliation.md): every iron, zinc, folate and B12 national estimate now reproduces its report to the decimal, and the Gambia LGA estimates track the report at r = 0.98 to 0.99. What changed then: the iron binaries had been the surveys' iron-deficiency-ANAEMIA columns in three countries (ferritin plus hemoglobin), Malawi's iron flag came from a mis-specified local BRINDA that under-counted by half, pregnant women and children outside 6 to 59 months were being kept, and vitamin A had been converted to retinol-equivalents with each survey's own RBP-to-retinol line. That conversion is now the sensitivity analysis, not the primary: the four lines were fitted in different directions on 14 to 300 specimens, and Malawi's has R-squared 0.13, which manufactures near-zero deficiency by construction; the survey's own re-analysis (Likoswe 2021) recommends exactly BRINDA-adjusted RBP below 0.70, the estimand used here. Call it low RBP rather than vitamin A deficiency: Ghana's MRDR found 6.7 percent depleted and Malawi's none. Two caveats to say if asked. Sierra Leone's child file as supplied holds only the survey's anaemic children (532 of 654 assayed), so its child outcome-country combinations are anaemic-subgroup estimates until the full file arrives. Folate is not comparable across the two assays (Malawi's microbiologic assay reads higher than the Roche immunoassay), so its cross-border numbers are indicative only. Iodine (The Gambia, Sierra Leone) is analyzed within country only; a one- or two-country outcome has no cross-border test.
:::

## What causes iron deficiency?

![](img/old_s06_framework_1.png){width="8.6in"}

::: {.notes}
SAY: The conceptual framework for iron deficiency: distal drivers at the top (ecology, climate, geography, economy), intermediate ones (food environment, care, infection), and the immediate causes at the bottom. The next slide colors the same boxes by whether we have a public proxy for them.

DETAIL: Adapted from Hess et al., Ann N Y Acad Sci 2023. The framework is unchanged; the ablation slides show which of its pathways the data can see.
:::

## Where do we have proxy data for those causes?

```{r framework-coverage, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.4, dpi=140}
fw <- data.frame(
  tier = c(rep("Distal drivers", 5), rep("Underlying risk factors", 5), rep("Intermediate risk factors", 5), rep("Direct causes", 4)),
  box = c("Physiological vulnerability\n(age, pregnancy)", "Ecology, climate,\ngeography", "Economy, politics", "Culture, norms", "Health policies",
          "Poverty", "Low education", "Limited health\nservices", "Inadequate\nsanitation, water", "Food insecurity,\nlow diversity",
          "Infectious disease,\nmalaria, helminths", "Inflammation", "Gynecological,\nobstetric conditions", "Inadequate iron\nintake (diet)", "Care practices,\ninfant feeding",
          "Inadequate absorption", "Increased losses\n(blood loss)", "Increased\nrequirements", "Inherited red-cell\ndisorders"),
  cover = c("Partly", "Yes", "Partly", "No", "Partly", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Partly", "Partly", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Partly", "Partly", "Yes"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fw$tier <- factor(fw$tier, levels = rev(c("Distal drivers", "Underlying risk factors", "Intermediate risk factors", "Direct causes")))
fw <- fw |> group_by(tier) |> mutate(x = (row_number() - 0.5) / n()) |> ungroup()
ggplot(fw, aes(x, tier)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = cover), width = 0.18, height = 0.78, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = box), size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Yes = "#a6d96a", Partly = "#fee08b", No = "#e0e0e0"), name = "Public proxy in the set", breaks = c("Yes", "Partly", "No"),
                    labels = c("Yes: district layers", "Partly: national or modeled only", "No")) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(0.02)) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The same boxes, colored by whether the 575 public predictors cover them. Green: we have district-level layers (climate, soil, poverty, water, malaria, diet from budget surveys). Yellow: only a national figure or a modeled surface. Gray: nothing public reaches it, which is culture, absorption and the individual physiology. The model can only see the green and yellow pathways.

DETAIL: Coverage judged from the domain list: ecology and climate (GEE, SoilGrids, AlphaEarth), poverty and education (MICS, HCES, GDL, RWI), sanitation and water (MICS, IHME WASH), food insecurity and diet (HCES food groups, HFID, FEWS, RTFP prices, MapSPAM, livestock), infection (Malaria Atlas, ESPEN helminths, IHME), care practices (MICS infant feeding), inherited red-outcome-country combination disorders (Malaria Atlas HbS, HbC, G6PD allele surfaces). Partly: physiological vulnerability and gynecological conditions (fertility and age structure from MICS/WorldPop), economy and policy (national constants, fortification standards), inflammation (only through malaria and diarrhea surfaces), losses and requirements (fertility, helminths). No: culture and norms, absorption. Likely question: is the lack of a culture proxy why the model plateaus. Possibly; it is one reason the deck says the vocabulary is saturated with respect to what is public.
:::
# The proxy dataset

## What do the land, climate and agriculture layers look like?

::: {.notes}
SAY: The land side of the data: what the satellites and soil surveys see. Rainfall and temperature normals, soil chemistry, crops, livestock, land cover and a satellite embedding, every one of them public and covering every district. The maps are Ghana, so you can see the north-south gradient most of these layers share.

DETAIL: Sources: Earth Engine TerraClimate (monthly climate, 4 km, survey year and 1991-2020 normals), MODIS (land-surface temperature, NDVI, EVI), Copernicus land cover, night lights, GHSL built-up, MODIS productivity, AlphaEarth 64-band satellite embedding, SoilGrids and iSDA soil chemistry at two depths, Koppen and agro-ecological zones, JRC surface water and coast distance, MapSPAM 2010 crop production and area, Gridded Livestock of the World 4, WorldPop, GHSL and GPW population, Meta relative wealth index. What a proxy has to be: This talk is about the right-hand side of the model: where the `r Q$n` columns come from, how each one gets from its native form to a district value, how we line them up with four surveys taken in four different years, and which of them the model leans on. The analysis deck covers what the ranking achieves; this one covers what it is made of. The leakage rule is the second bullet: a district aggregate of the same survey instance we score is excluded (docs/findings, LK-02), and where a MICS or DHS was fielded inside the biomarker survey's own clusters those clusters are dropped from the aggregate (The Gambia 2018: 70 MICS clusters; Malawi 2015-16: 105 DHS clusters). The record behind the fourth bullet is the shared metadata file and results/tables/protocol_v2/variable_sheet.csv. One consequence of the first bullet: `r Q$n_const` of the `r Q$n` columns are national series with one value per country, and a value that is the same in every district cannot rank districts, so the models drop them when they are fitted.
:::
## What do the health, food and household layers look like?

::: {.notes}
SAY: The people side: modeled health surfaces from IHME and the Malaria Atlas, helminths from WHO, food prices from WFP and the World Bank, and the public household surveys, MICS and the budget surveys, aggregated to districts. These are public too; the DHS is kept out of the headline models on purpose.

DETAIL: Sources: IHME 5 km modeled surfaces (child growth, anemia, WASH, education, ORS, HIV, measles vaccination), Malaria Atlas (parasite rate, incidence, mortality, nets, spraying, blood-disorder allele frequencies), WHO ESPEN helminth treatment coverage, WHO anemia and UNICEF vitamin A supplementation national series, WFP and World Bank real-time market prices, FAOSTAT balances and HFID food security, GFDx fortification standards, MIMI dietary inadequacy for Ghana, MICS microdata aggregated to districts, household budget surveys (IHS 2015/16, GLSS7, IHS4, SLIHS 2018) for diet, Global Data Lab HDI. DHS aggregates exist for all four countries and are a sensitivity arm only.
:::
## Where do the `r Q$n_pred` predictors come from?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- `r Q$n` predictors from `r Q$n_src` sources, every one matched to the same list of `r Q$n_spine` districts.
- `r if (!is.null(MD)) sum(MD$n_countries == 4) else 510` exist in all four countries, so they can serve a model for a new country.
- The other `r if (!is.null(MD)) sum(MD$n_countries < 4) else 60` exist in one to three and are used only inside those countries.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r sources, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=5.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(MD)) {
  d <- df(Source = source_label(MD$source), Coverage = ifelse(MD$n_countries == 4, "In all four countries", "In one to three countries")) |> count(Source, Coverage, name = "n")
  tot <- tapply(d$n, d$Source, sum); d$Source <- factor(d$Source, levels = names(sort(tot))); d$Coverage <- factor(d$Coverage, levels = c("In all four countries", "In one to three countries"))
  ggplot(d, aes(n, Source, fill = Coverage)) + geom_col(width = 0.72, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    geom_text(data = df(Source = factor(names(tot), levels = levels(d$Source)), n = as.vector(tot)), aes(n, Source, label = n), inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.2, size = 3.4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`In all four countries` = BLUE, `In one to three countries` = LIGHT)) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
    labs(x = "Predictors (label = total)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Twenty-eight sources, 575 predictors, one district list. Most are satellite and modeled surfaces; the public household surveys, MICS and the budget surveys, are the rest. The dark part of each bar exists in all four countries and can travel to a new one.

DETAIL: Read the bar chart from the top. One harmonized set feeds every model: the in-country models use whatever a country has, the cross-country models the columns all four share, so the light segment (household budget survey diet items for two countries, RTFP prices for two, MIMI for Ghana, MICS items missing from one round, a few IHME surfaces) works at home and not abroad. Behind the set sits a larger extraction: about 740 columns per country in the raw files (1,968 distinct names across the four, mostly the same quantity under country-specific names), harmonized to a common vocabulary; what did not harmonize was used only in the pre-protocol models. The Earth Engine block is climate (TerraClimate at the survey year and as 30-year normals), land cover, night lights, built-up surface, vegetation and evapotranspiration, night-time land surface temperature; the satellite embedding is Google's AlphaEarth, 64 numbers per district that summarize a year of imagery; soil is iSDA and SoilGrids, ten nutrient concentrations at two depths plus texture and pH; crops are MapSPAM's 2010 allocation; livestock is GLW4. The health and nutrition surfaces are IHME's modeled estimates (anemia, child growth, WASH, education, ORS, HIV, malaria, vaccination) and the Malaria Atlas layers; ESPEN gives helminth endemicity. Prices come from WFP markets, the World Bank's RTFP panel and FAOSTAT balances; fortification from GFDx. The public microdata blocks are new since 15 September: 30 indicators from the MICS files for all four countries and 15 diet and consumption indicators from the household budget surveys (IHS 2015/16, GLSS7, IHS4, SLIHS 2018). The DHS block is 150 district aggregates from the round paired with each survey (Ghana 2014, Malawi 2015-16, Sierra Leone 2013, The Gambia 2019-20), estimated with a cluster-level spatial model so every district has a value. Everything here is listed with its source, year and definition in results/tables/protocol_v2/variable_sheet.csv and in the dashboard's catalog.
:::

## How are the layers matched to districts in space and time?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Two rules. In space: one list of districts, and every layer is joined to it by a code, never by a district's name, so a renamed or split district cannot silently drop out. In time: every layer is taken at the year of the country's survey or the nearest year available, climate as a 30-year normal plus that year's anomaly, and the gap between the layer's year and the survey's is recorded for every column.

DETAIL: Space: The spine is metadata/admin2_spine.csv; the helpers in R/admin2_keys.R do every join in the pipeline and a lint test (tests/testthat/test-admin2-join-lint.R) reads every script for a join on a bare Admin2 name. The p-codes came from OCHA's COD-AB for all four countries this week, both directions, so an OCHA-coded source (IPC, ACLED, cluster surveys) joins without any matching. Fuzzy matching, where it is still needed, is Jaro-Winkler with a 0.15 cap and a review file that lists every non-exact match for a human to accept. The population defect: the dashboard's population table had been deduplicated by district name, so Chikwawa's TA Lundu and Nsanje's TA Ngabu, Salima's TA Pemba and Zomba's TA Malemia lost one member each, two of them surveyed districts, and every population-weighted figure silently excluded them. Fixed 15 September from WorldPop density, and the population table is now asserted complete in the tests. Time: The rules live in metadata/covariates/temporal_alignment.csv, `r if (!is.null(AL)) length(unique(AL$rule_id)) else 45` of them, one regular expression each: survey_year where an annual series exists (TerraClimate, MODIS NDVI, MAP, WorldPop density, WFP prices, RTFP windows), nearest available year where a series ends early (IHME's child growth, education and WASH stop at 2017, anemia and malaria at 2019), a fixed vintage where there is only one (AlphaEarth 2017, MapSPAM 2010, GLW 2015, RWI 2019), a per-country round for the household surveys, and static for soil, terrain, climate normals and zones. Climate and greenness enter as a 30-year normal plus the survey-year anomaly in standard-deviation units, which is what transports; the calendar-year series that lagged the survey by up to eight years were retired. Sierra Leone's 2013 survey is the awkward one: AlphaEarth starts in 2017, Copernicus land cover in 2015, and the MICS round nearest it is 2017, so its gaps are the orange and red bands. Ghana's are the DHS block: the round paired with the 2017 survey is the 2014 DHS, three years off for 140 columns. The gaps that apply everywhere are the single-vintage products: MapSPAM 2010, GLW 2015, WorldPop's 2020 age-sex structure. The stamp is per column and per country (results/tables/predictor_alignment_2026-09-16.csv), and the audit lists everything three or more years off.
:::
## `r Q$n_dom` conceptual domains of proxy variables

::: {.notes}
SAY: Twenty-nine domains, grouped here into eight for the slide, with the number of predictors in each. Each domain enters the model as its leading principal components rather than as raw columns, because 575 columns against 14 to 87 districts cannot be fitted one by one.

DETAIL: Why domains: `r Q$n` columns against 14 to 87 districts per country cannot be fitted column by column, and the columns are heavily correlated within a source. Grouping them by what they measure and taking principal components inside each group keeps most of the variance of each group, treats a source with 64 columns and a source with 3 as one construct each, and keeps the outcome out of the representation: the rotations are learned from the training districts' predictors alone, so nothing is selected on the biomarker. The grouping is written down: each source block brings a label, and `r if (!is.null(OV)) nrow(OV) else 10` override rules in metadata/covariates/domain_overrides.csv regroup columns by construct (infection and inflammation burden, immunisation, anemia, child anthropometry, infant feeding, supplementation, water and sanitation, education, child mortality, assets), so that MAP, IHME, DHS and MICS versions of the same thing are weighed together. Two things went wrong this week and are now guarded. A domain's first twelve characters are its key inside the model; two labels that shared them ("Food prices (RTFP)" and "Food prices and supply") were silently merged in two analyzes until a check caught it on 16 September. The other is in the exclusions, on the next slide. One more point for questions: climate alone or soil alone transports better than all domains together, the analysis deck's climate-and-soil result.
:::

## How is the district table built?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Six steps: clean the surveys to one definition per nutrient; link the gridded layers to districts; aggregate the household surveys; align everything in time; keep only open data in the headline models; then rank-normalize within country and reduce each domain to its leading components. Nothing in the last step looks at the outcome.

DETAIL: Why 28 sources but 29 domains: a source is where a layer comes from (IHME, the Malaria Atlas, MICS), a domain is what it measures; several sources feed one domain (malaria columns from MAP, IHME and MICS sit together) and one source feeds several domains (IHME supplies anemia, child growth and WASH). The column counts at each step are in the appendix CONSORT table.
:::

# Models and protocol

## Which algorithms did we compare?

::: {.notes}
SAY: A library of candidate algorithms, from a simple mean through penalized regressions, random forests, gradient boosting and spatial and geostatistical models, to the one that won: a principal-component index with nothing tuned. All are compared on the same honest folds.

DETAIL: The comparison run (SL-01 to SL-05, rerun on the current set): on identical district-blocked folds the PC index scores `r f2(Q$sl_index)` against `r f2(Q$sl_rank)` for the rank-loss SuperLearner ensemble, `r f2(Q$sl_rf)` for random forest, `r f2(Q$sl_mse)` for the squared-error ensemble, `r f2(Q$sl_hapc)` for the principal-component highly adaptive ridge and `r f2(Q$sl_enet)` for the elastic net (mean of outcome-country combination medians over `r Q$sl_cells` outcome-country combinations, prevalence, in-fill). Why the simplest wins: with 14 to 87 districts every estimator that tunes a parameter shrinks toward the constant under squared-error cross-validation; the index has no tuned parameter.
:::

## How do we choose among algorithms?

::: {.notes}
SAY: By ensemble machine learning, SuperLearner: every algorithm in the library is scored on data it did not see, with folds cut by district so no district is split between training and validation, and the best one, or the best weighted combination, is chosen. The principal-component index is one candidate in that library, and it is the one that wins.

DETAIL: No penalty other than computation to add a learner: diversity, redundancy, synergy. Library: mean, penalized regressions, random forest, gradient boosting, PCA-HAL, BART, geostatistical models, the PC index. Discrete SuperLearner picks the single best learner by cross-validated loss; the weighted version combines them. The figure on the right is the V-fold scheme.
:::

## How does the best-performing model work?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Four steps, none of which looks at a held-out district: rank every predictor within its country; take the leading components of each domain; weight each component by how well it tracks the outcome in the training districts; add them up. It is a weighted sum with the weights read off the data, nothing tuned.

DETAIL: Four steps, none of which looks at a held-out district. (1) Rank-normalize every predictor within country, so a level offset between surveys cannot act as signal. (2) Take the leading principal components of each of the `r Q$n_dom` domains, to 80% of variance and at most twelve, on the training districts. (3) Weight each component by its rank correlation with the outcome in the training fold, sign and size; nothing else is fitted. (4) Sum, and rescale to the training outcome spread. The index is the infinite-penalty limit of a ridge regression on the components (weighting slide in the appendix), and because it is linear in the rank-normalized columns every column has an exact back-projected weight, which is what the importance slides show.
:::

## Three levels of prediction

::: {.notes}
SAY: Three questions a program might ask, each tested by holding out the right thing. District in-fill: a district the survey missed in a country it did visit. Region extrapolation: a whole region the survey never reached. Cross-country transport: a country with no biomarker survey at all. Each is compared with the best thing you could do without the model.

DETAIL: In-fill folds are 5-fold by district repeated ten times; the baseline is the survey's own regional average computed without the held-out district (jackknifed) and a spatial smoother. Region extrapolation holds out one region at a time; baseline a spatial smoother. Transport holds out one country and trains on the other three; the baseline is a permutation null with country blocks kept intact. The earlier leaderboard compared transport-style models against an in-fill baseline that had seen the district's own respondents; that comparison is withdrawn. `r Q$null_pos95` of `r Q$tr_cells` combinations are positive at the 95th percentile of the null with no transport at all, so the mean correlation is what is compared with its null (`r f2(Q$null_d)` district, `r f2(Q$null_a1)` regional).
:::

## What is held out at each level?

```{r silhouettes, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.6, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  BND <- readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds")); LC <- c(Gambia = "gambia", Ghana = "ghana", Malawi = "malawi", SierraLeone = "sierraleone")
  shp <- lapply(names(LC), function(cn) { b <- sf::st_as_sf(BND[[LC[[cn]]]]); b$country <- cn; b }); names(shp) <- names(LC)
  # place the four countries on one canvas: translate each to a slot, scaled to a common height
  slot <- function(b, cx, cy, h = 1) { g <- sf::st_geometry(b); bb <- sf::st_bbox(g); sc <- h / (bb$ymax - bb$ymin); ctr <- c((bb$xmin + bb$xmax) / 2, (bb$ymin + bb$ymax) / 2)
    g2 <- (g - ctr) * sc + c(cx, cy); sf::st_sf(country = b$country, Admin1 = b$Admin1, Admin2 = b$Admin2, geometry = sf::st_sfc(g2)) }
  canvas <- rbind(slot(shp$Gambia, 0, 0.75, 0.35), slot(shp$SierraLeone, 0, -0.55, 0.9), slot(shp$Ghana, 1.6, 0.1, 1.5), slot(shp$Malawi, 3.0, 0.1, 1.9))
  set.seed(3); gh <- which(canvas$country == "Ghana"); ho_d <- sample(gh, 15); ho_r <- which(canvas$country == "Ghana" & canvas$Admin1 == canvas$Admin1[gh[1]])
  panel <- function(held, title, q, only_ghana = FALSE) { cv <- if (only_ghana) canvas[canvas$country == "Ghana", ] else canvas; cv$role <- ifelse(seq_len(nrow(canvas))[if (only_ghana) canvas$country == "Ghana" else TRUE] %in% held, "held out (predicted)", "training"); ggplot(cv) + geom_sf(aes(fill = role), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(training = "#1f4e79", `held out (predicted)` = "#f0a050"), name = NULL) + labs(title = title, subtitle = q) + theme_void(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30", size = 10), legend.position = "bottom") }
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(panel(ho_d, "District in-fill", "unsurveyed districts in a surveyed country", TRUE), panel(ho_r, "Region extrapolation", "a whole region the survey never reached", TRUE),
                              panel(which(canvas$country == "Ghana"), "Cross-country transport", "a country with no biomarker survey"), ncol = 3) + patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The same three levels as pictures: orange is predicted from blue. A few districts held out inside Ghana; a whole region of Ghana; then all of Ghana, predicted from the other three countries.

DETAIL: In-fill holds out districts one fold at a time (5-fold by district, ten draws); region extrapolation holds out a whole region; transport holds out a whole country and trains on the other three. Every fold is cut at the district or above, never through a district's respondents.
:::

# Results

## Where does the ranking work, outcome by outcome and country by country?

```{r cells-rank, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=6.0, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(CELL)) {
  est_lab <- c(infill = "In-fill (5-fold by district)", region = "Region extrapolation", country = "Country transport")
  ord <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> arrange(spearman_m)
  sl <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "country", arm == "domain_index", target == "level", !cell %in% ord$cell) |> arrange(spearman_m)   # Sierra Leone: transport only, at the foot
  lev <- c(sl$cell, ord$cell)
  d <- CELL |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% c("domain_index", "region_mean_jk", "spatial", "spatial_plus_domain", "domain_enet"), country != "SierraLeone" | estimand != "infill", arm %in% c("domain_index", "region_mean_jk")) |>
    mutate(what = case_when(arm == "domain_index" ~ "Best model (the index)", TRUE ~ "Survey's regional average"))
  d <- d |> mutate(cell = factor(cell, levels = lev), Estimand = factor(est_lab[estimand], levels = est_lab),
    strong = cell %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT])
  ggplot(d, aes(spearman_m, cell)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey55") + geom_vline(xintercept = STRONG_CUT, linetype = 3, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbarh(data = d |> filter(what == "Best model (the index)", is.finite(spearman_se)), aes(xmin = spearman_m - 1.96 * spearman_se, xmax = spearman_m + 1.96 * spearman_se), height = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(aes(shape = what, colour = what, fill = what, size = what)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`Best model (the index)` = 21, `Survey's regional average` = 4), name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Best model (the index)` = "#1f4e79", `Survey's regional average` = "grey40"), name = NULL) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Best model (the index)` = "#1f4e79", `Survey's regional average` = NA), name = NULL) +
    scale_size_manual(values = c(`Best model (the index)` = 2.8, `Survey's regional average` = 2.4), name = NULL) +
    facet_wrap(~ Estimand) + scale_y_discrete(limits = lev) + labs(x = "Spearman correlation, held-out districts, biomarker level (mean over draws, 95% interval)", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "#1f4e79", "grey35"), face = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "bold", "plain")))
}
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The average hides a spread. Each row is one outcome in one country; the filled point is the model, the cross the survey's own regional average. Six of the eighteen combinations clear 0.5 and average 0.64, in bold; the rest average 0.28. The failures are rare outcomes, zinc, and single-cluster districts; The Gambia, with several clusters per district, is strong on three of four outcomes.

DETAIL: Sierra Leone has no in-fill row: with 14 districts a 5-fold split leaves eleven to train on, below the twelve the protocol requires, so its in-fill score is NA and it is scored under region and country transport only. The averages elsewhere in this deck hide a spread that matters: `r Q$strong_n` of the `r Q$strong_of` in-country outcome-country combinations reach a held-out Spearman of `r f2(Q$strong_cut, 1)` or more on the biomarker level (mean `r f2(Q$strong_mean)`, bold on the axis), the rest average `r f2(Q$weak_mean)`. Rows are the country-outcome outcome-country combinations sorted by the index's in-fill ranking; the filled point is the deployed model with its interval over the ten fold draws, the cross is the survey's own regional average (the number a ministry would use), the hollow circle is the best of the other arms (spatial smoother, smoother plus covariates, elastic nets) picked on the same held-out score, so it is optimiztic and shown only to say how much a different estimator could have added: little. The middle and right panels are the region and country estimands for the same outcome-country combinations. The weak outcome-country combinations are of two kinds: outcomes too rare to measure at district level (Malawi's vitamin A outcome-country combinations at under 1% national prevalence: `r Q$rare_n` outcome-country combinations, mean `r f2(Q$rare_mean)`) and zinc (Malawi only, mean `r f2(Q$zinc_mean)`), where the survey's own district estimates carry almost no signal to recover; The Gambia, with 30 large districts and several clusters in each, clears the line on `r Q$gambia_strong` of its `r Q$gambia_cells` outcomes and scores `r f2(Q$gambia_min)` on the fourth (child iron), above the other countries' average; the next slides show the same outcome-country combinations on the prevalence and concentration scales, and the scatter after them puts the weak outcome-country combinations against their prevalence. Sierra Leone's 14 districts are not scored in-fill.
:::

## How far off is the predicted prevalence, outcome by outcome?

```{r cells-prev, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.4, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(CELL)) {
  ord <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> arrange(spearman_m)
  d <- CELL |> filter(target == "prev", estimand == "infill", arm %in% c("domain_index", "region_mean_jk"), is.finite(wmae_m)) |>
    mutate(what = case_when(arm == "domain_index" ~ "Best model (the index)", arm == "region_mean_jk" ~ "Survey's regional average", TRUE ~ "One national number"))
  d <- d |> mutate(cell = factor(cell, levels = ord$cell))
  lv <- c("Best model (the index)", "Survey's regional average")
  ggplot(d, aes(wmae_m, cell)) +
    geom_errorbarh(data = d |> filter(what == lv[1], is.finite(wmae_se)), aes(xmin = wmae_m - 1.96 * wmae_se, xmax = wmae_m + 1.96 * wmae_se), height = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(aes(shape = what, colour = what, fill = what), size = 2.7) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 4) |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1f4e79", "grey40") |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1f4e79", NA) |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = ord$cell) + labs(x = "Mean absolute error of the held-out district prevalence, percentage points (population-weighted)", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "#1f4e79", "grey35"), face = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "bold", "plain")))
}
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Same combinations, now the level: how many percentage points each district's predicted prevalence is from the survey's. The model is no better than the regional average here, and only a little better than one national number, because it is built to order districts, not to measure them.

DETAIL: Same combinations, same order, prevalence scale: the population-weighted mean absolute error of each district's held-out prevalence, in percentage points. Three references: the survey's own regional average, one national number for every district (the status quo where no sub-national estimate exists), and the best other arm chosen after the fact. Read the error against the outcome: an error of 10 points on an outcome at 40% is a different thing from 3 points on one at 4%, which is why the rare-outcome combinations look accurate here and useless on the ranking slide. The index is rescaled to the training districts' spread, so it is not built to minimize this error; the geostatistical comparator slide shows what a model that estimates a level and shrinks toward it does to absolute error. Where a level has to be defended, this slide plus the national anchor is the argument, not the ranking correlation.
:::

## How far off is the predicted mean concentration, outcome by outcome?

```{r cells-level, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.4, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(CELL)) {
  ord <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> arrange(spearman_m)
  d <- CELL |> filter(target == "level", estimand == "infill", arm %in% c("domain_index", "region_mean_jk"), is.finite(rmse_sd_m)) |>
    mutate(what = case_when(arm == "domain_index" ~ "Best model (the index)", arm == "region_mean_jk" ~ "Survey's regional average", TRUE ~ "One national number"))
  d <- d |> mutate(cell = factor(cell, levels = ord$cell))
  lv <- c("Best model (the index)", "Survey's regional average")
  ggplot(d, aes(rmse_sd_m, cell)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
    geom_errorbarh(data = d |> filter(what == lv[1], is.finite(rmse_sd_se)), aes(xmin = rmse_sd_m - 1.96 * rmse_sd_se, xmax = rmse_sd_m + 1.96 * rmse_sd_se), height = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(aes(shape = what, colour = what, fill = what), size = 2.7) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 4) |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1f4e79", "grey40") |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1f4e79", NA) |> stats::setNames(lv), name = NULL) +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = ord$cell) + labs(x = "RMSE of the held-out district mean log concentration, relative to its spread (1 = the national mean does as well)", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11),
      axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "#1f4e79", "grey35"), face = ifelse(levels(d$cell) %in% ord$cell[ord$spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT], "bold", "plain")))
}
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The same on the biomarker concentration scale, as error relative to how much districts differ: one means no better than the national mean. The model sits near one in most combinations even where it ranks well, which is the same message: order, not level.

DETAIL: Same combinations, mean concentration scale: the district mean of the log biomarker concentration (ferritin, RBP, folate, B12, zinc), predicted with the district held out, scored as root-mean-square error divided by the spread of the observed district means, so that 1.0 means no better than giving every district the national mean and anything below it is skill. The index is a ranker rescaled to the training spread, so its squared error is often at or above 1 even in combinations where it ranks well; the spatial smoother, which shrinks toward neighbors, is usually the best other arm on this loss. That is the honest division of labour the geostatistical slide draws: the index for the order, a shrinking estimator for the level. Cells whose index error sits well below 1 (the strong combinations in bold) are the ones where the proxies carry enough signal to predict the concentration itself, not only its order.
:::

## Where do the rankings work?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
Where it works: iron, B12 and vitamin A where the deficiency is common, and everywhere the survey has several clusters per district.

Why not elsewhere: an outcome under 1% prevalence has nothing to rank, zinc carries no district signal, and a single-cluster district gives the survey too little to be compared with.
:::
::: {.column width="68%"}
```{r cells-scatter, fig.width=7.4, fig.height=5.2, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(CELL) && !is.null(NT)) {
  ix <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |>
    left_join(NT |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index") |> group_by(country, outcome) |> summarise(prev_nat = mean(prev_national, na.rm = TRUE), n_areas = max(n_areas), .groups = "drop"), by = c("country", "outcome")) |>
    mutate(strong = spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT, nutrient = sub("^(child|women)_", "", outcome), nutrient = c(iron = "Iron", vitA = "Vitamin A", folate = "Folate", b12 = "B12", zinc = "Zinc")[nutrient])
  ggplot(ix, aes(prev_nat, spearman_m)) + geom_hline(yintercept = STRONG_CUT, linetype = 3, colour = "grey55") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = spearman_m - 1.96 * spearman_se, ymax = spearman_m + 1.96 * spearman_se), width = 0, colour = "grey70") +
    geom_point(aes(size = n_areas, colour = nutrient), alpha = 0.9) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = cell), size = 3.1, colour = "grey20", max.overlaps = 30, box.padding = 0.35) +
    scale_x_log10(labels = scales::percent, breaks = c(0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7)) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6), name = "Surveyed districts") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Iron = "#1f4e79", `Vitamin A` = "#e08214", Folate = "#33a02c", B12 = "#6a3d9a", Zinc = "#8c510a"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "National prevalence of the deficiency (log scale)", y = "Held-out Spearman, biomarker level (in-fill)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "right", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Each point is one outcome in one country against how common the deficiency is. Above the line: iron, B12 and vitamin A where they are common enough to measure, and The Gambia everywhere. Below: the very rare outcomes, zinc, and the single-cluster countries. The model needs a survey that can see districts before it can be shown to rank them.

DETAIL: Each point is a country-outcome outcome-country combination: the index's in-fill ranking accuracy against how common the deficiency is nationally. Rarity hurts at the extreme: below 1% prevalence (Malawi's two vitamin A combinations, mean `r f2(Q$rare_mean)`) the survey finds a handful of deficient respondents per district and its district estimates are mostly zero, so no predictor can recover an order; at 2 to 4% (The Gambia's and Ghana's women's vitamin A) the ranking still works. Above that, the spread is about the survey more than the nutrient: The Gambia's 30 districts with several clusters each score `r f2(Q$gambia_min)` to `r f2(Q$gambia_max)` (`r Q$gambia_strong` of `r Q$gambia_combinations` above the line), Ghana's and Malawi's single-cluster districts are mixed (`r Q$other_strong` of `r Q$other_combinations`). Zinc (Malawi only, `r f2(Q$zinc_mean)`) is the other failure and is not a rarity problem: serum zinc is unadjusted, drawn under fasting rules that vary by cluster, and the survey's own district means are close to noise. Everything the deck claims about ranking rests on the combinations above the dotted line: `r Q$strong_n` of `r Q$strong_of`, iron, vitamin A where it is common, folate and B12, in three countries. Likely question: why not just report those. Because the cut is chosen on the same held-out scores, so the strong-outcome-country combination mean of `r f2(Q$strong_mean)` is a description, not a promise; the promise for a new country is the transport slide's pre-registered climate-and-soil index.
:::

## The strongest outcome-country combinations

::: {.notes}
SAY: The four best: Malawi B12 and three of The Gambia's outcomes, all at or near 0.7 on the ranking. The level column is the caution: even here the district prevalence error is no better than the survey's regional average. Strong on the order, not on the level.

DETAIL: The four best in-country outcome-country combinations on the held-out ranking, from benchmarks_v2_raw.csv (in-fill, biomarker level, mean over ten draws), with the same outcome-country combination's prevalence-target ranking, its population-weighted district prevalence error in percentage points and the national prevalence. These are the outcome-country combinations to show a country: the model is not a uniform `r f2(Q$infill_index)`, it is `r f2(Q$strong_mean)` where the outcome is common enough to measure and close to nothing where it is not. `r Q$strong_n` of `r Q$strong_of` combinations clear `r f2(Q$strong_cut, 1)`.
:::

## How well does the model rank districts inside a surveyed country?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Mean rank correlation over the outcome-country combinations, with a 95% interval. The model reaches `r f2(Q$infill_index)` against `r f2(Q$infill_jk)` for the survey's own regional averages (better in `r Q$infill_beats_jk` of `r Q$infill_paired`). In plain terms: it puts `r pc(Q$pairs_pct)` of district pairs in the survey's order, the regional averages `r pc(Q$pairs_jk)`, a random ordering 50%.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r infill, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(BC)) {
  d <- BC |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm %in% names(arm_label)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("target", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(arm_label[arm], levels = rev(arm_label)), Target = tlab[target])
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Target", null = 0, base = 15, xlab = "Rank correlation (mean, 95% interval)")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Inside a surveyed country, predicting each district with that district held out, the model's ranking correlates 0.40 with the survey's, against 0.31 for the survey's own regional averages and 0.39 for a smoother that only uses neighbors. Six district pairs in ten are in the survey's order; the regional average manages five and a half.

DETAIL: Cells: `r Q$infill_paired` on the level (Sierra Leone's outcome-country combinations score NA at 14 districts). On prevalence the index scores `r f2(Q$infill_index_p)` against `r f2(Q$infill_jk_p)`. The smoother with covariates fitted to its residuals scores `r f2(Q$infill_spd)`; covariates add `r sgn(Q$infill_index_minus_sp)` over the smoother alone on the level. The penalized fits score `r f2(Q$infill_enet)` (domain components) and `r f2(Q$infill_raw)` (all columns). Likely question: why the smoother does so well. Inside a surveyed country the covariates mostly reproduce a smooth surface that neighboring districts already provide; the value of the covariates is in unsurveyed regions and countries.
:::

## Ghana: survey, held-out prediction, extrapolation and uncertainty

```{r ghana-four, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=5.2, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  B <- sf::st_as_sf(readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["ghana"]])
  oof <- rd(VZ, "oof_women_iron.csv"); dep <- rd(VZ, "deploy_ghana_women_iron.csv"); oof <- oof[oof$country == "Ghana", ]
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, oof[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "pred", "n_psu")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2")) |> dplyr::left_join(dep[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "pred_fit", "pred_lo", "pred_hi")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  g$width <- g$pred_hi - g$pred_lo
  sc <- scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, max(c(g$y_prev, g$pred_fit), na.rm = TRUE)), na.value = "grey90", name = NULL)
  th <- theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(0.9, "cm"))
  rho <- cor(g$y_prev, g$pred, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
  p1 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = y_prev), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "Survey 2017\n(surveyed districts)") + th
  p2 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = sprintf("Held-out prediction\n(rank correlation %.2f)", rho)) + th
  p3 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred_fit), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "Extrapolated to every district\n(fitted on the surveyed ones)") + th
  p4 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = width), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greys", direction = 1, labels = scales::percent, na.value = "grey90", name = NULL) + labs(title = "Uncertainty: width of the\n90% band over 200 refits") + th
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 4)); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Ghana, women's iron deficiency, one outcome across the four questions a map has to answer. Left, what the survey measured, district by district. Second, what the model predicts for each of those districts when it is held out. Third, the model applied to every district including the ones never surveyed. Right, how much each district's prediction moves when the training districts are resampled.

DETAIL: Panel 2 is the in-fill out-of-fold prediction (5-fold by district, ten draws, prevalence target). Panel 3 is the deployment fit: the index on all surveyed districts, applied to all, in-sample for the surveyed ones. Panel 4: 200 stratified resamples of the surveyed districts, the index refitted and applied each time; the width is the 90% band of predicted prevalence. Gray in panels 1 and 2: no survey clusters. The band measures stability under resampling, not distance from the truth (calibration slide). Tables: viz/oof_women_iron.csv, viz/deploy_ghana_women_iron.csv.
:::
## A whole unsurveyed region: the ranking holds at `r f2(Q$region_index)`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Leave-one-region-out, mean over outcome-country combinations with a 95% interval. The index scores `r f2(Q$region_index)` on the level and `r f2(Q$region_index_p)` on prevalence; the penalized fits fall to `r f2(Q$region_enet_p)` and `r f2(Q$region_raw_p)` on prevalence.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r region, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(BC)) {
  d <- BC |> filter(estimand == "region", arm %in% names(arm_label)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("target", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(arm_label[arm], levels = rev(arm_label)), Target = tlab[target])
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Target", null = 0, base = 15)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Leaving out a whole region is where a smoother must extrapolate past the edge of its data. The index and the smoother stay close (`r f2(Q$region_index)` against `r f2(Q$region_sp)` on the level); the null training mean collapses. Ghana and Malawi are the countries where this estimand is well determined; The Gambia and Sierra Leone give one number per region.
:::

## Does the model work in a country it has never seen?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Leave-one-country-out, `r Q$tr_cells` outcome-country combinations. The full index scores `r f2(Q$tr_index)` at district level (positive in `r Q$tr_index_pos` of `r Q$tr_cells`) and `r f2(Q$tr_a1)` at regional level; the climate-and-soil index scores `r f2(Q$cs_d)` and `r f2(Q$cs_a1)`. Dashed lines are the 95th percentile of the permutation null.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r transport, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=6.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(BC) && !is.null(A1) && !is.null(ND) && !is.null(CS1)) {
  d <- bind_rows(
    BC |> filter(estimand == "country", arm %in% c("domain_index", "domain_enet")) |> transmute(tier = "District", target, model = arm_label[arm], spearman),
    ND |> filter(arm == "fixed_cs") |> transmute(tier = "District", target, model = "Climate + soil index", spearman),
    A1 |> filter(arm == "domain_index") |> transmute(tier = "Regional", target, model = arm_label["domain_index"], spearman),
    CS1 |> filter(set == "climate_soil") |> transmute(tier = "Regional", target, model = "Climate + soil index", spearman)) |>
    cell_ci("spearman", c("tier", "target", "model")) |>
```
