```{r transport, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=6.2, dpi=160}
    mutate(Target = tlab[target], row = factor(paste(tier, model, sep = ": "), levels = rev(c("District: Zero-tuning domain index", "District: Elastic net, domain components", "District: Climate + soil index", "Regional: Zero-tuning domain index", "Regional: Climate + soil index"))))
  nulls <- df(tier = c("District", "Regional"), null = c(Q$null_d, Q$null_a1))
  p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(est, row)) + geom_vline(data = nulls, aes(xintercept = null), linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, colour = "grey35", orientation = "y") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f4e79") +
    facet_wrap(~ Target) + labs(title = "Rankings carry", x = "Rank correlation in the held-out country (mean, 95% interval)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  lv <- TG |> filter(outcome %in% c("women_iron", "child_vitA"), is.finite(y_level), is.finite(n_raw)) |> group_by(country, outcome) |> summarise(m = weighted.mean(-y_level, n_raw), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(Country = clab[country], Outcome = c(women_iron = "Women's ferritin", child_vitA = "Children's RBP")[outcome])
  p2 <- ggplot(lv, aes(m, Country)) + geom_point(size = 3.2, colour = "#d7301f") + facet_wrap(~ Outcome, scales = "free_x") + labs(title = "Levels do not", x = "National mean log concentration, survey", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(1.6, 1)))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Trained on three countries and applied to the fourth, the ranking carries: 0.30 with the full set of predictors, 0.38 with climate and soil alone, against 0.08 by chance. The level does not: the bottom panel shows why, the surveys' national mean biomarker concentrations differ several-fold, so a transported prevalence would be wrong before it started. What crosses a border is the order of districts.

DETAIL: Absolute levels do not transport: raw ferritin differs several-fold between surveys, so the transported product is a ranking. Prevalence: `r f2(Q$tr_index_p)` at district level (`r Q$tr_index_pos_p` of `r Q$tr_cells` positive) and `r f2(Q$tr_a1_p)` at regional level for the full index; `r f2(Q$cs_d_p)` at district level for climate and soil. The climate-and-soil pair was chosen on these four countries, so it enters the next country as a pre-registered prediction; honest nested selection of domains inside the training fold gives a median difference of `r sgn(Q$nested_vs_full)` from the full index (better in `r Q$nested_better` of `r Q$tr_cells`). DA-03 (17 September, RR-12 set): adding the next load-bearing domains of the ablation to climate and soil (anemia surfaces, agriculture, infection: five domains) reaches `r f2(Q$cs5_d)` at district level (better than climate-and-soil in `r Q$cs5_better` of `r Q$tr_cells`, median `r sgn(Q$cs5_delta)`, all 22 outcome-country combinations positive; `r f2(Q$cs5_d_p)` on prevalence), with the gain in the weak outcome-country combinations (women's iron and folate in Ghana and Sierra Leone) and none in the strong ones. It is chosen on the same 22 outcome-country combinations, so it goes into the pre-registration as a second candidate beside climate-and-soil, not in its place; the honest nested selection still sits at `r f2(Q$nested_d)` (next slide). Since 9 September the DHS-derived predictors are cluster-level spatial estimates at every district (DS-01), which changed nothing in-country and cost the full index 0.01 across borders. Likely question: what a correlation of `r f2(Q$tr_index)` means for a program. The targeting slide answers in burden captured.
:::

## Can the transport model be improved by adding domains?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Leave-one-country-out, `r Q$tr_cells` outcome-country combinations, mean with a 95% interval across outcome-country combinations. Climate and soil alone: `r f2(Q$cs_d)`. Adding the next load-bearing domains of the ablation (anemia surfaces, agriculture, infection) reaches `r f2(Q$cs5_d)` (better in `r Q$cs5_better` of `r Q$tr_cells`, median `r sgn(Q$cs5_delta)`). Chosen on these same outcome-country combinations, so a candidate for the next country, not a replacement. Honest nested selection: `r f2(Q$nested_d)`.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r cs-domains, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(ND)) {
  lab <- c(fixed_cs = "Climate + soil (pre-registered)", fixed_cs_anaemia = "+ anaemia surfaces", fixed_csa = "+ agriculture", fixed_cs_landscape = "+ agriculture, livestock, greenness",
           fixed_cs_top5 = "+ anaemia, agriculture, infection", fixed_loadbearing = "All load-bearing domains", nested = "Chosen inside the training fold (honest)", full = "Full index, all domains")
  d <- ND |> filter(arm %in% names(lab)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("target", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)), Target = tlab[target])
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Target", null = Q$null_d, base = 13, xlab = "Spearman in the held-out country (mean, 95% interval)")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Adding the next load-bearing domains, the anemia surfaces, agriculture and infection, to climate and soil raises transport from 0.38 to 0.41. That set was chosen on the same countries it is scored on, so it becomes a second candidate to test on the fifth survey, not a replacement.

DETAIL: Dashed line: the 95th percentile of the permutation null. DA-03 (17 September, RR-12 set): script 25 scores fixed domain sets on the same leave-one-country-out folds as the transport slide, with the domain components oriented on the training countries only. The five-domain set (climate, soil, anemia and hemoglobin, agriculture and land use, infection and inflammation) is the top of the ablation ranking on these outcome-country combinations: `r f2(Q$cs5_d)` at district level against `r f2(Q$cs_d)` for climate and soil, positive in all `r Q$tr_cells` outcome-country combinations, `r f2(Q$cs5_d_p)` against `r f2(Q$cs_d_p)` on prevalence. The gain is in the weak outcome-country combinations (women's iron and folate in Ghana and Sierra Leone) and absent in the strong ones. Because the set was chosen from the ablation on these same 22 outcome-country combinations, it has the same status as climate-and-soil had when it was found: a description of these four countries, to be scored as a second pre-registered candidate on the fifth. The honest arm, domains chosen by an inner leave-one-country-out inside the three training countries, stays at `r f2(Q$nested_d)`: with two inner folds the greedy choice overfits, which is why the pre-registration route is the one that can settle this. Likely question: why not use all load-bearing domains. All eight load-bearing domains score `r f2(Q$load_d)`; nothing beyond five adds.
:::

## What does the model say for Cote d'Ivoire, which has no survey?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="24%"}
Children's iron, from climate and soil layers only. The model has never seen a Cote d'Ivoire biomarker.

Left: which districts to reach first. Right: how firmly each is placed, the width of the 90% rank range over 400 refits on resampled training districts (median `r f2(Q$civ_med_width, 0)` places out of `r Q$civ_n`; the five worst-ranked stay in the worst third every time).
:::
::: {.column width="76%"}
![](../../results/figures/policy_deck/fig10_civ_ranking.png){width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Cote d'Ivoire is the case the project exists for: the public layers, no biomarker survey. The index trained on the four surveyed countries ranks its 33 districts, and the northern savanna belt comes out worst, the drier, poorer, more pastoral half of the country. The right map says how firmly: most districts move only a few places when the model is refitted on different training districts.

DETAIL: Cote d'Ivoire has the climate and soil layers and no biomarker survey, so it is the case the project exists for. The climate-and-soil index was fitted on the four surveyed countries and applied to its `r Q$civ_n` districts for `r Q$civ_outcomes` outcomes (child and women's iron and vitamin A, women's folate and B12); it has never seen a Cote d'Ivoire biomarker. Left: child iron; the worst-ranked districts are the northern savanna belt (Tchologo, Bounkani, Bagoue, Poro, Hambol), the drier, poorer, more pastoral half of the country. Right: how firmly each district is placed. The training set was resampled 400 times, stratified by country, the components re-oriented and the index refitted each time, and the district re-ranked; the map shows the width of the 90 percent range of ranks, median `r f2(Q$civ_med_width, 0)` places out of `r Q$civ_n`. `r Q$civ_hi` of `r Q$civ_n` districts have at least an 80 percent chance of being in the worst third and `r Q$civ_lo` at most 20 percent. What this uncertainty covers: how much the ranking depends on which training districts we learned from. What it does not cover: whether the model transports to Cote d'Ivoire at all, because there is no ground truth there; the external bound on that is the held-out transport accuracy of `r f2(Q$cs_d)`. Two guards ran first: the same code with each surveyed country held out reproduces the transport figure (`r f2(Q$civ_guard4)` over `r Q$civ_guard4_n` outcome-country combinations, `r Q$civ_guard4_pos` positive), and adding Cote d'Ivoire to the column intersection costs `r Q$civ_cols4 - Q$civ_cols5` of the `r Q$civ_cols4` climate-and-soil columns (the few layers the Cote d'Ivoire extraction lacks) without degrading transport (`r f2(Q$civ_guard5)`, `r Q$civ_guard5_pos` positive). CV-01 (17 September): the Cote d'Ivoire database was extended from 132 to `r 132 + Q$civ_new_cols` columns with the open rasters the other domains need (IHME surfaces, Malaria Atlas at 2016, MapSPAM, livestock, and the 30-year climate normals that were missing), so the climate-and-soil index now runs on its full vocabulary (`r Q$civ_cols5` common columns, guard `r f2(Q$civ_guard5)`) and the five-domain candidate can be applied too (next slide). Rank uncertainty is now computed for all six outcomes and both candidates (civ_rank_uncertainty_all.csv). The only external check so far is the WFP/MIMI Nature Food 2026 vitamin A map, which ranks the same northern belt worst. Tables: civ_climate_soil_ranking.csv, civ_rank_uncertainty.csv, civ_transport_guards.csv.
:::
## How much of the burden does the worst-ranked fifth reach?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
If a program went to the fifth of districts the model ranks worst, what share of the country's deficient people would it reach? On average `r pc(Q$cap_index)`, against `r pc(Q$cap_jk)` for the survey's regional averages and `r pc(Q$cap_oracle)` with perfect knowledge; the dashed line is a random fifth. Right: the same for the six strongest outcome-country combinations.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r burden, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=4.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(NT) && !is.null(CELL)) {
  lab <- c(oracle_ceiling = "Perfect knowledge", domain_index = "Best model (the index)", region_mean_jk = "Survey's regional average", null_train_mean = "One national number")
  strong_cells <- CELL |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm == "domain_index", target == "level", spearman_m >= STRONG_CUT) |> mutate(key = paste(country, outcome)) |> pull(key)
  d <- NT |> filter(estimand == "infill", arm %in% names(lab)) |> group_by(country, outcome, arm) |> summarise(v = mean(capture_top20, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(set = ifelse(paste(country, outcome) %in% strong_cells, "Six strongest combinations", "All 24 combinations"))
  d <- bind_rows(d |> mutate(set = "All 24 combinations"), d |> filter(set == "Six strongest combinations")) |> cell_ci("v", c("set", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)), set = factor(set, levels = c("All 24 combinations", "Six strongest combinations")))
  ggplot(d, aes(est, Model)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, colour = "grey35", orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f4e79") + facet_wrap(~ set) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    labs(x = "Share of the national deficiency burden in the fifth of districts ranked worst (mean, 95% interval)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: A program that goes to the fifth of districts the model ranks worst reaches about a fifth of the deficient people, a little more than the survey's own regional averages would, and less than half of what perfect knowledge would give. Even in the six strongest combinations the gain over the regional average is small: burden sits in populous districts, and the ranking is not a burden map.

DETAIL: The dashed line is the share a random fifth of districts would capture. The margin over the survey's own regional averages is small per outcome-country combination and concentrates where regions hold three to five districts. Under transport, burden captured is at chance: the transported product is an ordering and brings no targeting gain. Likely question: why the ceiling is only `r pc(Q$cap_oracle)`. Burden is spread across districts; even the true worst fifth holds under half of it.
:::

## How good are the models? One table, two readings

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r eval-summary}
if (!is.null(BC)) {
  bo <- BC |> filter(arm == "domain_index") |> group_by(outcome, estimand, target) |> summarise(v = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), m = mean(wmae, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  tab <- bo |> filter(target == "level", estimand %in% c("infill", "country")) |> select(outcome, estimand, v) |> pivot_wider(names_from = estimand, values_from = v) |>
    left_join(bo |> filter(target == "prev", estimand == "infill") |> select(outcome, mae = m), by = "outcome") |>
    transmute(Outcome = olab[outcome], `Ranking, surveyed country` = round(infill, 2), `Ranking, new country` = round(country, 2), `District error (points)` = round(mae, 1)) |> arrange(desc(`Ranking, surveyed country`))
  kb(tab, digits = 2)
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
**Ranking.** For every pair of districts, the survey says which is worse and so does the model, predicting each district with it held out. They agree on `r pc(Q$pairs_pct)` of pairs inside a surveyed country: six in ten, against five in ten for a random ordering and `r pc(Q$pairs_jk)` for the best you can do with survey data alone, the region's average. In a country the model has never seen, `r pc(Q$pairs_pct_tr)`.

**Level.** Inside a surveyed country a district's predicted prevalence is off by `r f2(Q$oof_mae_Gambia, 0)` to `r f2(Q$oof_mae_Ghana, 0)` percentage points on average (child iron), no better than the region's average. In a new country, one small national sample (5% of a survey) plus the ranking gives `r f2(Q$ar_a1, 1)` points; a district survey needs `r pc(Q$ar_b_match)` of its full size to match that. Read levels as planning figures; the ranking is the product.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: One table and two sentences. The table: for each outcome, how well the model ranks districts inside a surveyed country and in a new one, and how far off its district prevalence is. The sentences: it gets six district pairs in ten in the survey's order, against five and a half for the region's average; and a level is only trustworthy with a national anchor.

DETAIL: The MIMI deck's evaluation summary format: the per-outcome table on the left (held-out Spearman inside a country and in a new country, biomarker level; the population-weighted district prevalence error in-fill), and on the right the two sentences a policy reader takes away, one about the order and one about the level, with the pair-count and the anchor error behind them. The four draft translation slides that follow expand these two readings; keep this one if only one fits.
:::

## What does a rank correlation of `r f2(Q$infill_index)` mean on the ground?


::: {.notes}
SAY: Three readings of the same 0.40, all from the best model, the index, predicting each district with it held out: six pairs in ten in the survey's order; the flagged fifth has a third more deficiency than the country; that fifth holds a fifth of the deficient people. Real, modest, and better than the number a ministry has today.

DETAIL: DRAFT A of four candidate translations; all numbers are the index (the deployed and best-performing model), averaged over the 24 outcome-country combinations; in the six strongest combinations the pair count is about 70%. The three readings are all computed from the same held-out predictions (in-fill, 5-fold by district, ten draws). Pairs: counted exactly from the held-out predictions (12_nce_targeting_metrics.R, PC-01: every pair of districts, ties excluded, mean over the 24 outcome-country combinations): the model orders `r pc(Q$pairs_pct)` of district pairs the way the survey does, the survey's own regional averages `r pc(Q$pairs_jk)`, a coin toss 50%; across borders (leave-one-country-out, `r Q$pairs_tr_cells` outcome-country combinations) it is `r pc(Q$pairs_pct_tr)`. A Spearman of `r f2(Q$infill_index)` sounds like more than it is: at district level it is six pairs in ten. The flagged fifth: deficiency prevalence in the fifth of districts the model ranks worst averages `r f2(Q$top20_prev_index, 1)`% against `r f2(Q$top20_prev_nat, 1)`% nationally (nce_targeting_summary.csv, mean over the 24 outcome-country combinations); a map that knew the truth would find `r f2(Q$top20_prev_oracle, 1)`%. Burden: the model's worst fifth holds `r pc(Q$cap_index)` of the deficient people, the survey's own regional averages `r pc(Q$cap_jk)`, a perfect map `r pc(Q$cap_oracle)`. The honest message is that the ranking is real but modest: it is better than the regional average a ministry would use today, and a long way from a map that knows every district, which is what the reliability ceiling explains.
:::

## How much of what a survey can see does the model recover?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Two comparisons that make 0.40 readable. First, against the ceiling: the survey's own district estimates are noisy, so even a perfect predictor would only reach 0.48 against them; the model reaches 59% of that. Second, against the best prediction you can make with survey data alone, the region's average: the model beats it in 13 of 18 combinations.

DETAIL: How the ceiling is known: a variance model with respondents nested in clusters, clusters in districts and districts in regions, fitted to each survey, gives the share of district-to-district variation that is true signal rather than sampling noise; the correlation a predictor of the true value could reach with the observed value follows from that share (variance_components_ceiling.csv). The regional average is jackknifed: each district's value is its region's average computed without that district's own respondents, so it never sees the answer. DRAFT B. The question a decision-maker actually asks is not "is 0.40 high" but "compared with what". Two comparisons. Against the ceiling: a district estimate from the survey itself is noisy (one to three clusters per district), so even a perfect predictor of the true prevalence would correlate only `r f2(Q$vc_honest)` with what the survey reports; on that scale the model's `r f2(Q$infill_index_p)` (prevalence target) is `r pc(Q$ceiling_share)` of the attainable. Against current practice: the number a ministry would use for an unsurveyed district today is its region's average; the model beats it (`r f2(Q$infill_index)` against `r f2(Q$infill_jk)`, better in `r Q$infill_beats_jk` of `r Q$infill_paired` outcome-country combinations). Say plainly that the remaining gap is mostly the survey's noise, not the model's ignorance, and that the way to raise the ceiling is more clusters per district, which is the survey-design slide.
:::

## Does the model put districts in the right severity band?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Policy runs on severity bands. With each district held out, the model puts 64% of districts in the survey's WHO vitamin A band and 91% within one band. The survey's regional averages do slightly better, because a band is mostly a level; the model's case is a band where there is no survey at all.

DETAIL: DRAFT C. Policy runs on severity bands, not correlations: WHO's vitamin A bands are under 2%, 2 to 10, 10 to 20, 20% or more. With each district held out, the model puts `r pc(Q$rc_ex)` of districts in the band the survey puts them in and `r pc(Q$rc_w1)` within one band (risk_category_accuracy.csv, mean over the vitamin A outcome-country combinations); the survey's own regional averages give `r pc(Q$rc_jk_ex)` exact and `r pc(Q$rc_jk_w1)` within one band. Read the comparison honestly: on severity bands the survey's own regional averages do as well as the model or slightly better, because a band is mostly a level and the regional average carries the country's own level. The model is almost never two bands wrong (a district the survey calls severe is not called mild), and its case is not that it beats the regional average on bands but that it gives a band where there is no survey at all; in a new country the level comes from the national anchor (risk-class slide in the appendix has the transport rows). Use this slide only if the audience reads vitamin A or anemia severity maps, and say the regional-average comparison aloud rather than letting the numbers sit.
:::

## Which decisions are our models good enough for?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Which districts to visit first, where the next survey should sample, the order of a roll-out: yes. A planning prevalence: only with a national anchor. A district prevalence with no survey, or whether a program worked: no.

DETAIL: DRAFT D. The correlation does not tell a program whether the model is fit for a decision; this slide says which decisions, and which not. Yes: choosing which districts to visit, assess or enrol first, and where the next survey should put its clusters, because those need an order and the order is `r pc(Q$pairs_pct)` right at the pair level and better than the regional average. Yes: sequencing a roll-out across districts, for the same reason. With a national anchor only: a planning prevalence per district (`r f2(Q$ar_a1, 1)` points median error at a 5% national sample), because the ranking has no level of its own. No: reporting a district prevalence with no survey at all, or judging whether a program worked, because the model is cross-sectional and validated on levels at one point in time, not on change. The decision rule to offer: use it where being roughly right about the order is enough, and pair it with a survey wherever a number has to be defended.
:::

## Malawi: survey, held-out prediction, extrapolation and uncertainty

```{r malawi-four, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=5.2, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  B <- sf::st_as_sf(readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["malawi"]])
  oof <- rd(VZ, "oof_women_iron.csv"); dep <- rd(VZ, "deploy_malawi_women_iron.csv"); oof <- oof[oof$country == "Malawi", ]
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, oof[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "pred", "n_psu")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2")) |> dplyr::left_join(dep[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "pred_fit", "pred_lo", "pred_hi")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  g$width <- g$pred_hi - g$pred_lo
  sc <- scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, max(c(g$y_prev, g$pred_fit), na.rm = TRUE)), na.value = "grey90", name = NULL)
  th <- theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(0.9, "cm"))
  rho <- cor(g$y_prev, g$pred, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
  p1 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = y_prev), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "Survey 2015-16\n(surveyed districts)") + th
  p2 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = sprintf("Held-out prediction\n(rank correlation %.2f)", rho)) + th
  p3 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred_fit), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + sc + labs(title = "Extrapolated to every district\n(fitted on the surveyed ones)") + th
  p4 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = width), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greys", direction = 1, labels = scales::percent, na.value = "grey90", name = NULL) + labs(title = "Uncertainty: width of the\n90% band over 200 refits") + th
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 4)); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Malawi, women's iron deficiency, one outcome across the four questions a map has to answer. Left, what the survey measured, district by district. Second, what the model predicts for each of those districts when it is held out. Third, the model applied to every district including the ones never surveyed. Right, how much each district's prediction moves when the training districts are resampled.

DETAIL: Panel 2 is the in-fill out-of-fold prediction (5-fold by district, ten draws, prevalence target). Panel 3 is the deployment fit: the index on all surveyed districts, applied to all, in-sample for the surveyed ones. Panel 4: 200 stratified resamples of the surveyed districts, the index refitted and applied each time; the width is the 90% band of predicted prevalence. Gray in panels 1 and 2: no survey clusters. The band measures stability under resampling, not distance from the truth (calibration slide). Tables: viz/oof_women_iron.csv, viz/deploy_malawi_women_iron.csv.
:::
# Seeing the results

## How should every map in this deck be read?

::: {.notes}
A convention borrowed from the small-area-estimation literature (hatching for direct estimates whose coefficient of variation exceeds a third; gray for no data). Every district on every map in this deck belongs to one of three grades. A: surveyed with several clusters, so the survey's own district estimate is worth comparing with; `r Q$multi_n` districts. B: surveyed with one cluster, the majority (`r pc(Q$single_share)` of surveyed districts), where the survey's district number is itself an estimate with the noise the ceiling slide quantifies; hatched wherever a survey value is drawn. C: no survey clusters, where only the model speaks; gray on survey maps, filled on model maps. The grade says what the map can be compared against, not how good the model is.
:::

## How reliable is the survey's own district map?

```{r hatched-maps, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.4, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  BND <- readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))
  hatch <- function(g, flag, step = 0.08) {   # diagonal lines clipped to the flagged polygons
    h <- g[flag, ]; if (!nrow(h)) return(NULL); bb <- sf::st_bbox(h); L <- list(); k <- 1
    for (c0 in seq(bb$xmin - (bb$ymax - bb$ymin), bb$xmax, by = step)) { L[[k]] <- sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(c0, bb$ymin), c(c0 + (bb$ymax - bb$ymin), bb$ymax))); k <- k + 1 }
    lines <- sf::st_sfc(L, crs = sf::st_crs(h)); suppressWarnings(sf::st_intersection(sf::st_geometry(sf::st_union(h)), lines)) }
  one <- function(lc, cn, title) {
    B <- sf::st_as_sf(BND[[lc]]); t <- TG[TG$country == cn & TG$outcome == "child_iron", c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "n_psu")]
    ce <- if (is.null(VC)) NA else get1(VC$ceiling_vc[VC$rung == "admin2" & VC$target == "prev" & VC$country == cn & VC$outcome == "child_iron"])
    g <- dplyr::left_join(B, t, by = c("Admin1", "Admin2")); g$grade <- ifelse(is.na(g$y_prev), "C: no survey clusters", ifelse(g$n_psu > 1, "A: several clusters", "B: one cluster"))
    hb <- hatch(g, g$grade == "B: one cluster")
    p <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = g, aes(fill = y_prev), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) + scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, na.value = "grey90", name = "Child iron deficiency\n(survey)")
    if (!is.null(hb)) p <- p + geom_sf(data = hb, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.35)
    p + labs(title = title, subtitle = sprintf("A %d districts (several clusters)   B %d hatched (one cluster)   C %d gray (no survey)\nReliability ceiling: a perfect predictor would correlate %.2f with this map", sum(g$grade == "A: several clusters"), sum(g$grade == "B: one cluster"), sum(g$grade == "C: no survey clusters"), ce)) +
      theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"), legend.position = "right") }
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(one("ghana", "Ghana", "Ghana, survey 2017"), one("malawi", "Malawi", "Malawi, survey 2015-16"), ncol = 2)); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Before judging the model, look at what it is judged against. Hatched districts have one survey cluster; their value is one cluster's respondents. The number under each title is the ceiling: how well a perfect predictor of the true district value could correlate with this map. Around 0.5 to 0.7. That is the bar, not 1.0.

DETAIL: The survey's own district map of child iron deficiency, with the reliability grades drawn on it. Hatched districts have one survey cluster: their value is a single cluster's respondents, and the split-half ceiling says how much of the district-to-district variation on this map is noise. Unhatched districts have several clusters. Gray districts have none. When the next slides compare the model with "the survey", this is the survey they compare with; the model's job is to be a better estimate of the true district value than a single hatched cluster is, which the reliability-ceiling slide shows it can be in the strong outcome-country combinations.
:::

## Does the model track the survey, district by district?

```{r pred-obs, fig.width=11.5, fig.height=4.6, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(OOF)) {
  d <- OOF |> mutate(Country = clab[country], grade = ifelse(n_psu > 1, "several clusters", "one cluster"))
  st <- d |> group_by(Country) |> summarise(lab = sprintf("Spearman %.2f\nMAE %.1f points\n%d districts", cor(y_prev, pred, method = "spearman"), 100 * mean(abs(y_prev - pred)), n()), .groups = "drop")
  ggplot(d, aes(y_prev, pred)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pred_lo, ymax = pred_hi), width = 0, colour = "grey75") + geom_point(aes(shape = grade, size = n_raw), colour = "#1f4e79", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = st, aes(x = 0.02, y = Inf, label = lab), hjust = 0, vjust = 1.2, size = 3.3, colour = "grey20") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`several clusters` = 16, `one cluster` = 1), name = NULL) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 5), name = "Respondents") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + facet_wrap(~ Country, scales = "free") +
    labs(x = "Survey estimate of child iron deficiency", y = "Held-out prediction (bar: range over draws)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```

::: {.notes}
The plot every geostatistical paper carries and this deck lacked: each district's survey estimate against its prediction made with the district held out (5-fold by district, mean over ten draws; the bar is the range over the draws, which is fold-assignment variability, not sampling error). The dashed line is perfect agreement. Read three things. The cloud is tilted, not on the line: the model ranks (Spearman `r f2(Q$oof_rho_Ghana)` in Ghana, `r f2(Q$oof_rho_Gambia)` in The Gambia, `r f2(Q$oof_rho_Malawi)` in Malawi) but compresses the range, because it is rescaled to the training spread and shrinks extremes, which is the MAE of `r f2(Q$oof_mae_Ghana, 1)` to `r f2(Q$oof_mae_Malawi, 1)` points. Hollow points are single-cluster districts: much of the vertical scatter around them is the survey's noise, not the model's. The largest circles, the districts with the most respondents, sit closest to the line.
:::

## Does it match the survey at the regional level?

```{r admin1-pairs, fig.width=11.5, fig.height=5.2, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  BND <- readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds")); LC <- c(Gambia = "gambia", Ghana = "ghana", Malawi = "malawi")
  a1 <- OOF |> group_by(country, Admin1) |> summarise(Survey = weighted.mean(y_prev, n_raw), Predicted = weighted.mean(pred, n_raw), .groups = "drop")
  maps <- list()
  for (cn in names(LC)) { B <- sf::st_as_sf(BND[[LC[[cn]]]]) |> group_by(Admin1) |> summarise(geometry = sf::st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop")
    g <- dplyr::left_join(B, a1[a1$country == cn, ], by = "Admin1") |> tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Survey, Predicted), names_to = "panel", values_to = "value") |> mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Survey", "Predicted")))
    rho <- cor(a1$Survey[a1$country == cn], a1$Predicted[a1$country == cn], method = "spearman")
    maps[[cn]] <- ggplot(sf::st_as_sf(g)) + geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) + facet_wrap(~ panel) + scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, name = NULL) +
      labs(title = sprintf("%s: %d regions, Spearman %.2f", clab[cn], nrow(B), rho)) + theme_void(base_size = 11) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(1, "cm")) }
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(maps, ncol = 3)); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
The same held-out district predictions, and the survey, both aggregated to the regions (respondent-weighted means), child iron. This is the resolution at which the surveys were designed to be read, and the comparison a ministry statistician will make first. The regional pattern is recovered in each country; the district slide before this one shows the finer level where the survey itself becomes noisy. The MIMI and IHME decks show exactly this pair of maps as their headline validation figure.
:::

## How likely is a district to be above the 20% line?

```{r exceedance-map, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.4, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  B <- sf::st_as_sf(readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["ghana"]])
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, EXC, by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  p1 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = pred_med), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) + scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent, name = "Predicted\nprevalence") + labs(title = "Predicted prevalence (median of the refits)") + theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  p2 <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = p_ge20), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#fff7bc", mid = "#f0a050", high = "#7a0177", midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1), name = "P(prevalence >= 20%)") +
    labs(title = "Probability of exceeding the WHO severe band (20%)") + theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, ncol = 2)); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
The device IHME uses for every one of its maps, applied here: not "what is the prevalence" but "how likely is it to be above the line a program acts on". Ghana, child vitamin A, the index fitted on the 75 surveyed districts and applied to all `r Q$exc_n` (in-sample for the surveyed ones), refitted on `r Q$exc_refits` stratified resamples of the training districts; the right map is the share of refits in which a district's predicted prevalence is at or above 20 percent, the WHO severe band. `r Q$exc_hi` districts are above the line in at least 80 percent of refits, `r Q$exc_lo` below it in at least 80 percent, and `r Q$exc_mid` are undecided; `r Q$exc_unsurveyed` of the `r Q$exc_n` have no survey clusters. The level here comes from Ghana's own survey, so this is the in-country version; for a new country the level would come from the national anchor and the map would read as a planning figure. The caveat is the same as for the Cote d'Ivoire intervals: the refits capture how much the map depends on which training districts were drawn, not the survey's own noise at each district.
:::

## How bad, and how sure, on one map?

```{r bivariate-civ, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.6, dpi=140}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  B <- sf::st_read(file.path(root, "data", "external_cache", "gee_geoms", "civ_admin2.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, CU, by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  g$sev <- cut(g$rank_med, breaks = c(0, 11, 22, 33), labels = c("worst third", "middle", "best third"))
  g$cert <- cut(pmax(g$p_worst3rd, 1 - g$p_worst3rd), breaks = c(0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.001), labels = c("unsure", "fairly sure", "sure"), right = FALSE)
  g$cert[is.na(g$cert)] <- "sure"
  pal <- c("worst third.sure" = "#3b0f70", "worst third.fairly sure" = "#7b3294", "worst third.unsure" = "#c2a5cf",
           "middle.sure" = "#4d7fa3", "middle.fairly sure" = "#8bb5cc", "middle.unsure" = "#d4e3ec",
           "best third.sure" = "#1b7837", "best third.fairly sure" = "#7fbf7b", "best third.unsure" = "#d9f0d3")
  g$key <- paste(g$sev, g$cert, sep = ".")
  m <- ggplot(g) + geom_sf(aes(fill = key), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
    geom_sf_text(data = g[g$sev == "worst third" & g$cert == "sure", ], aes(label = Admin2), size = 3, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
    labs(title = "Children's iron: which districts to reach first, and how firmly each is placed") + theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  leg <- expand.grid(sev = c("worst third", "middle", "best third"), cert = c("unsure", "fairly sure", "sure")); leg$key <- paste(leg$sev, leg$cert, sep = ".")
  leg$n <- sapply(leg$key, function(k) sum(g$key == k))
  l <- ggplot(leg, aes(cert, sev, fill = key)) + geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) + geom_text(aes(label = n), size = 3.5, colour = "white") + scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = c("best third", "middle", "worst third")) + labs(x = "How sure (P of that third over 400 refits)", y = "Ranking (median)") + coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(m, l, widths = c(2.6, 1))); ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
The two Cote d'Ivoire maps folded into one, the bivariate device the geospatial-health literature recommends for policy audiences: color hue is the ranking (purple worst third, blue middle, green best third; median over the 400 refits) and color depth is how sure the refits are of that placement (deep = at least 80 percent of refits put it in that third; pale = under 60 percent). The legend counts districts in each outcome-country combination. The reading is immediate: deep purple, act; pale purple or pale blue, survey first; deep green, lowest priority. The labeled districts are the deep-purple ones, the northern belt. As before, "sure" means stable under resampling of the training set, not verified against a Cote d'Ivoire survey.
:::

## What do the rank intervals promise, and what do they not?

```{r coverage, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(COV) && !is.null(DRK)) {
  d <- COV |> mutate(Outcome = olab[outcome], Country = clab[heldout])
  p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(coverage_90, Outcome)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.9, linetype = 2, colour = "#d7191c") +
    geom_point(aes(colour = Country, size = width_share), alpha = 0.9) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`The Gambia` = "#1f4e79", Ghana = "#e08214", Malawi = "#33a02c", `Sierra Leone` = "#6a3d9a"), name = "Held-out country") + scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 7), labels = scales::percent, name = "Interval width\n(share of list)") +
    labs(title = "How often the 90% resampling interval holds the survey rank", x = "Coverage (dashed: the nominal 90%)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
  w <- data.frame(what = c("Resampling interval (as drawn)", "Calibrated to 90% coverage", "A random ordering"), half = c(Q$boot_half, Q$cal90, 0.68))
  w$what <- factor(w$what, levels = rev(w$what))
  p2 <- ggplot(w, aes(half, what)) + geom_col(fill = c("grey60", "#1f4e79", "#d7191c")[c(3, 2, 1)], width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("\u00b1%.0f%% of the list", 100 * half)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.8) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(title = "Half-width a 90% interval needs, one district's rank", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, widths = c(1.3, 1)))
}
```

::: {.notes}
A calibration check the Cote d'Ivoire slides needed. The 90 percent rank intervals on those maps come from resampling the training districts. If they were honest intervals for the truth, the survey's own rank would fall inside them 90 percent of the time. Doing exactly that with each surveyed country held out (100 resamples of the other three, climate and soil, biomarker level), the survey rank falls inside the interval `r pc(Q$cov_mean)` of the time on average, `r pc(Q$cov_min)` to `r pc(Q$cov_max)` across the `r Q$cov_cells` country-outcome outcome-country combinations, with a median interval `r pc(Q$cov_width)` of the list wide. So the intervals are far too narrow to be read as "the truth is in here"; they answer a different question, how much the ranking would move if we had learned from different districts, and the gap to 90 percent is the model error the transport correlation already reports. Right panel: the calibrated width. Taking the 90th percentile of the distance between the held-out survey rank and the point prediction over all `r Q$cal_n` held-out districts (conformal calibration), a 90 percent interval for a single district's rank has to be `r pc(Q$cal90)` of the list either side, against `r pc(Q$boot_half)` for the interval as drawn and about 68 percent for a random ordering; the median miss is `r pc(Q$cal50)` of the list (random: 29 percent). In words: at a transport correlation of 0.3 to 0.4, an honest 90 percent interval on where one district sits is nearly the whole list, and it is `r pc(Q$cal90_gambia)` in The Gambia and `r pc(Q$cal90_malawi)` in Malawi. The useful statement is therefore not an interval but a probability of a class: a district the model puts in the worst third is in the survey's worst third `r pc(Q$hit3)` of the time (chance `r pc(Q$hit3_base)`), and one it puts in its top five `r pc(Q$hit5)` of the time. That is what the Cote d'Ivoire maps should be read as: deep color means the model will not change its mind, and a worst-third call is right about half the time rather than a third. Say it aloud: stable, not verified, and honest about the odds.
:::

## What moves each district, predictor by predictor?

```{r beeswarm, fig.width=11.5, fig.height=5.6, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(CTR)) {
  d <- CTR |> filter(outcome == "child_iron") |> mutate(name = ifelse(is.na(PLAIN[column]), clean_code(column), unname(PLAIN[column])))
  ord <- d |> group_by(name, rank) |> summarise(.groups = "drop") |> arrange(desc(rank)); d$name <- factor(d$name, levels = ord$name)
  d <- d |> group_by(column) |> mutate(xq = (rank(x) - 0.5) / n()) |> ungroup()
  ggplot(d, aes(contribution, name, colour = xq)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_jitter(height = 0.25, width = 0, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.75) + scale_colour_gradient(low = "#3b8ec2", high = "#d7191c", labels = c("low", "high"), breaks = c(0.05, 0.95), name = "Predictor value\n(within country)") +
    labs(x = "Contribution to the district's child iron index (right = ranks worse); one point per surveyed district, pooled four-country fit", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10.5), legend.position = "right")
}
```

::: {.notes}
The SHAP-style view the MIMI deck uses, which the index allows exactly rather than by approximation: the index is linear in the rank-normalized predictors, so each district's score is a sum of per-predictor contributions beta times x. One row per predictor (the twelve largest weights of the pooled child-iron fit), one point per surveyed district in the four countries, color = where the district sits on that predictor. A row whose red points sit to the right says "districts high on this predictor rank worse"; a row that is wide says the predictor separates districts strongly. Unlike the bar charts earlier, this shows the spread: a predictor with a modest average weight can still move a handful of districts a long way. The same figure exists for every outcome from contributions_top12.csv.
:::

## Does each survey added improve every other map?

```{r curve-argument, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(TC) && !is.null(TCS)) {
  d <- bind_rows(TC |> filter(arm == "domain_index", target == "level") |> transmute(set = "Full vocabulary", n_train_countries, spearman),
                 TCS |> filter(set == "climate_soil", target == "level") |> transmute(set = "Climate + soil", n_train_countries, spearman)) |>
    group_by(set, n_train_countries) |> summarise(m = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(spearman, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(spearman, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  ggplot(d, aes(n_train_countries, m, colour = set)) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.1) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Full vocabulary` = "#1f4e79", `Climate + soil` = "#e08214"), name = NULL) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) +
    labs(x = "Surveys the model learned from", y = "Ranking accuracy in a country it has never seen") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

::: {.notes}
The training-country curve from the transport section, re-captioned as the argument it makes: with one survey to learn from the transported ranking averages `r f2(Q$tc_n1)`, with three `r f2(Q$tc_n3)`, and the curve has not flattened. Every biomarker survey a country runs therefore improves the map of every other country in the panel, which is the case for pooling surveys into one protocol rather than analyzing each alone, and for the fifth country being worth more than its own map. Bars are the interquartile range over the subsets of training countries. This is the framing the Lancet Global Health vaccination-mapping paper uses for its country panel.
:::

# What carries the signal

## Which predictors carry the most weight?

```{r top-weights-one, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.2, dpi=150}
if (!is.null(IT)) {
  d <- IT |> filter(outcome == "child_iron", target == "level", rank <= 12) |>
    mutate(name = ifelse(is.na(PLAIN[column]), clean_code(column), unname(PLAIN[column])), name = factor(name, levels = rev(name)), dir = ifelse(beta_std > 0, "More of this: worse iron status", "More of this: better iron status"))
  ggplot(d, aes(abs(beta_std), name, fill = dir)) + geom_col(width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * share)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`More of this: worse iron status` = "#d7301f", `More of this: better iron status` = "#1f4e79"), name = NULL) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(x = "Weight in the pooled four-country index for child iron (label: share of the index carried)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10.5))
}
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The twelve heaviest predictors for child iron, pooled over the four countries, with plain names. Red bars mean more of the layer goes with worse iron status, blue with better. No single predictor carries more than a few percent of the index: it is a sum of many small signals, mostly about landscape and livelihoods, not one master variable.

DETAIL: The index is linear in the rank-normalized predictors, so its component weights project back exactly onto the columns (scripts 57 and 58); shown is the pooled fit on the biomarker level, labels from R/predictor_plain_names.R. The satellite embedding, climate and soil together carry `r pc(Q$env_lo)` to `r pc(Q$env_hi)` of the index depending on the outcome. The other outcomes are in results/figures/protocol_v2/index_importance_top10_level.png. Likely question: whether these are causes. They are not; the weights say where deficiency is.
:::
## What are the weights behind the best ranking? Malawi, women's B12

```{r vim-b12, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.6, dpi=150}
VF <- rd(root, "results", "tables", "policy_deck", "vim_forest_Malawi_women_b12.csv")
if (!is.null(VF)) {
  d <- VF |> filter(rank <= 20) |> mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(plain) | plain == "", label, plain), label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))
  ggplot(d, aes(median, label)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey55") + geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = domain), size = 3.2) + geom_point(aes(x = full), shape = 1, size = 3.2, colour = "grey20") +
    labs(x = "Weight in the district index (median and 5th to 95th percentile over 300 refits; hollow = full fit; right = worse B12 status)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 9), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10.5)) + guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 4))
}
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: The single best ranking in the study, women's B12 in Malawi, and the twenty predictors behind it. Districts where more infants are fed meat or fish, more households eat fish, and wealth is higher have better B12; poorer, grassier, more pastoral districts have worse. And then the anemia and malaria surfaces run the other way, which the next slide explains.

DETAIL: Malawi, women's B12, biomarker level: the outcome-country combination with the best in-fill ranking of the 24 (Spearman 0.70; The Gambia child vitamin A is next at 0.69). The index is linear in the rank-normalized columns, so every column has a standardized weight in a fit; the twenty largest are shown. Intervals: the index was refitted on 300 bootstrap resamples of Malawi's 87 surveyed districts, with the domain components re-oriented and the weights re-learned each time; the bar is the 5th to 95th percentile and the hollow marker the weight in the full fit. Every one of the twenty keeps its sign in at least 95 percent of refits. The level target is the negated log concentration, so a positive weight means worse status. Read the signs as district-level associations in Malawi: districts where more infants are fed meat or fish, more households ate fish last week and the wealth score is higher have better B12 status, and districts that are poorer, grassier, further from permanent water and with more pigs have worse. The diet items point the way a nutritional story would expect; the anemia and malaria surfaces run the other way (more anemia and malaria, better B12), which is the lakeshore and the south against the uplands, and a reminder that these are ecological associations, not effects. Script: scripts/policy_deck/09_vim_forest_example.R, which takes any country, outcome and target through environment variables. B12 is measured in three of the four surveys, so this outcome-country combination does not enter the cross-country transport figures.
:::
## Causal driver or surrogate marker? Fish, anemia and B12 in Malawi

```{r b12-surrogate, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.2, dpi=130}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  source(file.path(root, "R", "protocol_v2.R"))
  S  <- read.csv(file.path(root, "data", "covariates", "harmonized", "predictors_admin2_shared.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
  PREDS <- intersect(MD$column, names(S)); domain_of <- stats::setNames(MD$domain, MD$column)
  B <- readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["malawi"]]
  t <- TG[TG$country == "Malawi" & TG$outcome == "women_b12" & is.finite(TG$y_prev), c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev")]
  s <- S[S$country == "Malawi", c("Admin1", "Admin2", "ihme_allanemia", "hces_any_fish", PREDS)]
  m <- dplyr::left_join(s, t, by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))          # every district; y_prev NA where no survey clusters
  # the deployment fit: the index on all surveyed districts, applied to every district (as on the dashboard)
  tr <- which(is.finite(m$y_prev)); Xr <- prep_predictors_v2(as.matrix(m[, PREDS])); Y <- .v2_logit(m$y_prev)
  D <- domain_representation_v2(Xr, domain_of, sign_rows = tr)
  m$pred <- .v2_expit(ARMS_V2[["domain_index"]](tr, seq_len(nrow(m)), Y, NULL, D, list(Admin1 = m$Admin1, y_nat = Y)))
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, m[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "pred", "ihme_allanemia", "hces_any_fish")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  r1 <- cor(g$y_prev, g$ihme_allanemia, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"); r2 <- cor(g$y_prev, g$hces_any_fish, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
  pct <- function(x) 100 * (rank(x, na.last = "keep") - 1) / (sum(is.finite(x)) - 1)   # within-country percentile, so the maps share one scale
  labs4 <- c(y_prev = "Women's B12 deficiency\nsurvey 2015-16\n ", pred = "Model-predicted deficiency\nevery district, fitted on\nthe surveyed ones",
             ihme_allanemia = sprintf("Modelled anaemia\nin women (IHME)\nrho with B12 def. = %.2f", r1), hces_any_fish = sprintf("Households eating\nfish last week (IHS4)\nrho with B12 def. = %.2f", r2))
  long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(labs4), function(v) data.frame(g[, c("Admin1", "Admin2")], value = pct(g[[v]]), panel = labs4[[v]])))
  long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = labs4)
  print(ggplot(sf::st_as_sf(long)) + geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 4) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey92", name = "Percentile among Malawi districts (100 = highest)", limits = c(0, 100)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.6, "cm"), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, lineheight = 1.05), strip.clip = "off", panel.spacing.x = grid::unit(1.0, "cm")))
  ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
SAY: Some predictors are plausible causes, fish consumption for B12. Some are surrogates: the anemia and malaria surfaces predict better B12 in Malawi not because malaria protects anyone but because they mark the lakeshore and the south, where fish is eaten. The model finds both kinds; it cannot tell them apart, and a surrogate need not travel to the next country.

DETAIL: The story behind the forest plot on the previous slide. In Malawi the modeled anemia and malaria surfaces carry negative weights for B12: districts with MORE anemia and malaria have BETTER B12 status. No nutritional mechanism says that. The maps say why: the lakeshore and the southern lowlands are where malaria transmission and anemia are highest, and they are also where households eat fish, the main dietary B12 source in the country; the uplands have less malaria, less fish and worse B12. The anemia surface is a surrogate marker for that geography, not a cause, and it is a good one precisely because it is modeled from the same environment. Three lessons for the audience: the index finds these markers on its own, they are ecological associations and must never be read as effects, and a surrogate that works in Malawi need not work in the next country, which is why the cross-border models lean on climate and soil rather than on health surfaces (ablation slide). The second panel is the deployment fit (the index fitted on the 87 surveyed districts and applied to all 243, in-sample for the surveyed ones, as on the dashboard): it fills the gray districts and smooths the survey's single-cluster noise, and it visibly follows the anemia and fish geography. Each map is the within-country percentile of its variable so the four share one scale; rho is the Spearman correlation with B12 deficiency across the surveyed Traditional Authorities (negative for anemia and for fish: more of either, less deficiency).
:::

## What travels across borders, and what does not?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Loss in transported Spearman (biomarker level, `r Q$tr_cells` outcome-country combinations) when each domain is dropped and the components rebuilt, mean over outcome-country combinations with a 95% interval. The load-bearing domains are `r paste(head(Q$da_top$domain, 3), collapse = ", ")`; removing `r Q$da_neg` of the `r Q$da_n` domains costs nothing or helps.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r ablation, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=5.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(DA)) {
  d <- abl_delta(DA, "domain") |> filter(target == "level") |> cell_ci("delta", "domain") |> arrange(est) |> mutate(domain = factor(domain, levels = domain))
  forest(d, "domain", null = 0, base = 12, xlab = "Loss in transported Spearman when dropped (mean, 95% interval)")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: Drop each domain in turn and see what the transported ranking loses. Climate and soil are load-bearing; the anemia surfaces, agriculture and greenness follow; the household-survey items help inside a country and not across a border. The physical environment is what carries, and it is also what a country without a survey can download.

DETAIL: Positive values mean the domain is load-bearing. Climate and soil carry most, with the anemia surfaces, agriculture and greenness behind; the water-and-sanitation, education and infant-feeding domains sit at or below zero: removing them does not hurt a new country and in two cases helps. The DHS-derived domains are not in the headline set at all: with them in, the district transport index scores `r f2(Q$tr_dhs)` against `r f2(Q$tr_index)` without. A fixed climate-and-soil index transports at `r f2(Q$cs_d)` at district level and `r f2(Q$cs_a1)` regionally against `r f2(Q$tr_index)` and `r f2(Q$tr_a1)` for the full vocabulary; it was found on the same four countries it is scored on and enters the next country as a pre-registered prediction.
:::

## What drives the transport models?

::: {.notes}
Source: results/tables/protocol_v2/index_importance_columns.csv, scope "loco": the index fitted on three countries, projected back to columns, for each of the `r Q$loco_fits` held-out country and outcome combinations on the biomarker level; a column counts once per fit in which it is among the twenty largest standardized weights. Every column named on the slide keeps the same sign in every fit where it appears (`r if (!is.null(REC)) sum(REC$sign_agree[REC$n_fits >= 5] == 1) else NA` of the `r if (!is.null(REC)) sum(REC$n_fits >= 5) else NA` columns that recur in five or more fits are unanimous). The pattern is the one on the previous two slides seen from the other side: what a model trained elsewhere reaches for in a new country is the physical environment and the modeled nutrition surfaces built from it, not the country's own survey items. The staple-price and malaria signs are worth saying aloud: relatively expensive staples mark market-integrated, better-off districts, and high malaria transmission marks the wet, productive lowlands where diets are more diverse; neither is a mechanism to act on.
:::

## Which associations replicate in every country?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Indicators whose district-level association with the outcome has the same sign in every country with the outcome, ranked by pooled meta-analytic z. Positive z means more deficiency.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r signal, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=5.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(SIG)) {
  d <- SIG[SIG$sign_agree >= SIG$k_countries & SIG$k_countries >= 3 & SIG$group %in% c("child_vitA", "child_iron", "women_iron", "women_vitA"), ]
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(d, d$group), function(g) head(g[order(-abs(g$meta_z)), ], 4)))
  d$Outcome <- olab[d$group]; d$Direction <- ifelse(d$mu > 0, "More deficiency", "Less deficiency")
  nice <- function(v) { p <- ifelse(is.na(PLAIN[v]), clean_code(v), unname(PLAIN[v]))   # interpretable labels (R/predictor_plain_names.R), plus the coded families
    p <- ifelse(grepl("^lst_night_m[0-9]+$", v), sprintf("Night-time temperature, %s", month.name[as.integer(sub("^lst_night_m", "", v))]), p)
    p <- ifelse(grepl("^lst_day_m[0-9]+$", v), sprintf("Daytime temperature, %s", month.name[as.integer(sub("^lst_day_m", "", v))]), p)
    p <- ifelse(grepl("^aef_A[0-9]+$", v), sprintf("Satellite embedding, band %d", as.integer(sub("^aef_A", "", v))), p)
    p <- ifelse(grepl("^soil_[a-z]+_stdev_", v), sprintf("Soil %s, variability (%s cm)", sub("^soil_([a-z]+)_stdev_.*$", "\1", v), gsub("_", "-", sub("^soil_[a-z]+_stdev_", "", v))), p)
    p <- ifelse(grepl("^soil_[a-z]+_mean_", v), sprintf("Soil %s (%s cm)", sub("^soil_([a-z]+)_mean_.*$", "\1", v), gsub("_", "-", sub("^soil_[a-z]+_mean_", "", v))), p)
    p }
  d$plain <- nice(d$predictor)
  d$key <- factor(paste(d$plain, d$group), levels = paste(d$plain, d$group)[order(d$group, d$meta_z)])
  ggplot(d, aes(meta_z, key, colour = Direction)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") + geom_point(size = 3) +
    facet_wrap(~ Outcome, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) + scale_y_discrete(labels = function(k) sub(" [a-z_A-Z]+$", "", k)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("More deficiency" = "#b2182b", "Less deficiency" = "#2166ac")) +
    labs(x = "Strength of the association, pooled over countries (z)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Legume cultivation and cattle ownership track more deficiency at district level, the reverse of the household-level dietary relationship, which is an ecological-fallacy signature: the replicated axis is rural subsistence agro-ecology, useful for deciding where to look and uninformative about what to change. No malaria burden indicator replicates; child wasting tracks women's vitamin A deficiency in all four countries. An earlier version of these slides had the signs inverted.
:::

# Limits and survey design

## How good could any model be against this survey?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
The survey's own district numbers are estimates, mostly from one cluster each. This shows how well even a perfect predictor of the true district value could match them: on average `r f2(Q$vc_honest)`, by country. The model's `r f2(Q$infill_index_p)` on the same scale is `r pc(Q$ceiling_share)` of that. The gap between the model and 1.0 is mostly the survey's noise, not the model's ignorance.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r ceiling, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(VC)) {
  d <- VC |> filter(rung == "admin2", target == "prev") |> transmute(country, outcome, `Split-half ceiling` = ceiling_within_vc, `Honest ceiling` = ceiling_vc, `Achieved, in-fill` = achieved_spearman) |>
    pivot_longer(-c(country, outcome), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "v") |> group_by(country, quantity) |> summarise(v = mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("Split-half ceiling", "Honest ceiling", "Achieved, in-fill")), country = sub("SierraLeone", "Sierra Leone", country))
  ggplot(d, aes(v, country, colour = quantity, shape = quantity)) + geom_point(size = 3.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Split-half ceiling" = "grey55", "Honest ceiling" = "#1f4e79", "Achieved, in-fill" = "#b15928")) +
    labs(x = "Spearman correlation (mean over outcomes)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: A survey that samples one cluster per district gives a district number with a lot of noise in it. Even a model that knew the truth exactly would only correlate about 0.5 with that number. So when the model scores 0.4, it has most of what there is to get; the way to raise the bar is more clusters per district, which is a survey decision.

DETAIL: A respondent-in-cluster-in-district-in-region variance model reproduces the split-half ceiling when the cluster is counted as geography, then removes the cluster term: `r pc(Q$vc_share)` of the split-half ceiling was cluster effect. Child zinc has no district geography; what looked like geography was the cluster, and the time of the blood draw explains part of the cluster effect (ZN-02).
:::

## Could a small national survey plus the model replace a district survey?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Four ways to get district numbers, costed against the size of survey each needs. A small national sample, 5% of a full survey, with the model's ranking spread across districts gives a median district error of `r f2(Q$ar_a1, 1)` points. A survey designed to measure each district directly needs about `r pc(Q$ar_b_match)` of its full size to do as well.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r anchor, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(AR)) {
  lab <- c(A1_anchor_rank = "National anchor + ranking", A2_region_anchor_rank = "Regional anchors + ranking", B_district_survey = "District survey", C_regional_survey = "Regional survey")
  d <- AR |> filter(rank_from == "prev", set == "climate_soil", design %in% names(lab)) |> group_by(design, fraction) |>
    summarise(mae = median(mae, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(mae, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(mae, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(Design = lab[design])
  ggplot(d, aes(fraction, mae, colour = Design)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    labs(x = "Share of the full survey sample", y = "Median district error (percentage points)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SAY: On the level of deficiency, a small national sample plus the ranking does as well as a district survey four to five times its size. On finding where the deficient people are, a district survey of any size still wins, because it measures the populous districts directly. So: not a replacement, a much cheaper first pass.

DETAIL: A district survey matches the anchored ranking's level error at about `r pc(Q$ar_b_match)` of the full sample. The ranking wins on level error only: a district survey of any size captures more burden, because burden sits in populous districts that surveys measure precisely. Fitted symmetrically on a reduced survey, the model's error degrades in step with the survey's, so the model improves the ordering at any sample size and does not reduce the sample a survey needs.
:::

## Does each survey added help the others?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Every subset of training countries scored on each held-out country. The full vocabulary gains about `r f2(Q$tc_slope)` per added training country on the level; the climate-and-soil index starts higher and is positive in `r pc(Q$tcs_pos1)` of single-country fits.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r curve, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(TC) && !is.null(TCS)) {
  d <- bind_rows(TC |> filter(arm == "domain_index") |> mutate(set = "Full vocabulary") |> select(target, set, n_train_countries, spearman),
                 TCS |> filter(set == "climate_soil") |> mutate(set = "Climate + soil") |> select(target, set, n_train_countries, spearman)) |>
    group_by(target, set, n_train_countries) |> summarise(mean_rho = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(spearman, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(spearman, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(target = tlab[target])
  ggplot(d, aes(n_train_countries, mean_rho, colour = set)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.45) +
    facet_wrap(~ target) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Full vocabulary" = "#1f4e79", "Climate + soil" = "#b15928")) +
    labs(x = "Training countries", y = "Transported Spearman (mean, IQR)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Bars are the interquartile range over fits. Likely question: whether four countries are enough. The curve has not flattened at three training countries, which is the argument for adding surveys to the panel rather than changing the estimator.
:::

# Closing

## What the models can and cannot do yet

::: {.notes}
The checklist agreed at the 10 September check-in, one row per question. Sources: benchmarks_v2_summary.csv (in-fill and country transport, biomarker level), transport_null_calibration.csv (95th percentile of the permutation null), nested_domain_selection.csv (fixed climate-and-soil set), index_importance_domains.csv (pooled shares of the three remotely sensed domains), anchor_and_rank.csv (AR-01, 5% fraction, climate-and-soil set, ranks from prevalence), variance_components_ceiling.csv (prevalence, admin2). Levels do not transport because the surveys differ in year, season, team and calibration (fe_transport_level_offset); the anchor supplies the level the ranking lacks. Guiding the next survey is a design result on these four surveys, not a pilot.
:::

## What have we learned, and what comes next?

::: {.notes}
SAY: Public data can rank a country's districts by micronutrient deficiency: inside a surveyed country better than the survey's own regional averages, and in a country with no survey at all, where nothing else can. Where the survey resolves districts, the model is close to the best any model could be. A single national number puts a level on the ranking. The uncertainty on the maps is honest about what it is. Next: the fifth survey scores the two pre-registered indices, the survey design gets piloted, and every survey added improves every other country's map.

DETAIL: The rows are the numbers from the optimiztic reading (TWO_READINGS_2026-09g.md). Not on the slide, said if asked: the honest product is a ranking, levels remain planning figures, and the per-outcome maps in an unsurveyed country are mostly one map of environmental deprivation.
:::

## Sources, tiers and alignment

```{r source-table}
if (!is.null(MD)) {
  t <- MD |> mutate(Source = source_label(source)) |> group_by(Source) |>
    summarise(Columns = n(), Tier = paste(sort(unique(tier_lab)), collapse = "; "), `Domains` = length(unique(domain)),
              `Year rule` = paste(sort(unique(alignment_rule)), collapse = ", "), `Largest gap (years)` = if (all(is.na(year_offset_max_abs))) "static" else as.character(max(year_offset_max_abs, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(Columns)) |> mutate(`Year rule` = ifelse(nchar(`Year rule`) > 60, paste0(substr(`Year rule`, 1, 57), "..."), `Year rule`))
  kb(t, digits = 0)
}
```

Tier: open means downloadable by anyone; public survey microdata means a registration with the survey program; DHS means the DHS Program's access agreement. Year rule names are the rule identifiers in metadata/covariates/temporal_alignment.csv. The largest gap is the worst case over the four countries; static layers have none.
